chunks.source: ISRO Career Guide Jobs Exams Resources
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: ISRO CAREER GUIDE Jobs, Qualifications, Exams & Study Resources A practical guide for students and graduates in India | Updated: 9 October 2026 ISRO (Indian Space Research Organisation) recruits people for engineering, science, research, technical, administrative, medical and support roles. There is no single examination that every applicant must pass. The correct route depends on the post, discipline, qualification and recruitment notice.

chunks.source: ISRO Career Guide Jobs Exams Resources
chunks.heading: 1. Main ISRO job positions and job profiles
chunks.text:
- Scientist/Engineer — Mechanical/Aerospace: Typical work: Design and test launch vehicles, propulsion hardware, spacecraft structures, thermal systems and mechanisms; Typical study route (check each notice): B.E./B.Tech or other specified degree in Mechanical, Aerospace or an accepted related discipline; higher study may help for specialist roles.
- Scientist/Engineer — Electronics/ECE: Typical work: Develop satellite communication systems, antennas, sensors, navigation electronics, signal processing and onboard systems; Typical study route (check each notice): B.E./B.Tech in ECE, Electronics or an accepted equivalent discipline.
- Scientist/Engineer — Computer Science/IT: Typical work: Develop mission software, simulations, satellite data pipelines, ground systems, automation and secure computing; Typical study route (check each notice): B.E./B.Tech in CSE, IT or another discipline explicitly accepted in the advertisement.
- Remote Sensing / Earth Observation Scientist: Typical work: Interpret satellite imagery for agriculture, forests, water resources, oceans, mapping and disaster management; Typical study route (check each notice): Relevant engineering/science degree; some posts require a specified postgraduate degree in remote sensing, GIS, geoinformatics or a related field.

chunks.source: ISRO Career Guide Jobs Exams Resources
chunks.heading: 1. Main ISRO job positions and job profiles
chunks.text:
- Space Science Researcher: Typical work: Study planetary science, solar physics, astronomy, atmospheres, plasma and scientific data from space missions; Typical study route (check each notice): Often B.Sc. then M.Sc. in Physics, Mathematics, Astronomy/Astrophysics or a relevant field; Ph.D. for many independent research careers.
- Mission Operations / Flight Dynamics: Typical work: Support spacecraft tracking, orbit determination, trajectory analysis, mission planning and satellite manoeuvres; Typical study route (check each notice): Relevant degree in aerospace, mechanical, electronics, computer science, physics or mathematics, depending on the vacancy.
- Payload / Instrumentation Engineer or Scientist: Typical work: Develop cameras, spectrometers, sensors and scientific instruments carried by spacecraft; Typical study route (check each notice): Relevant degree in Physics, Optics, Instrumentation, ECE, Electrical or Mechanical Engineering, as specified.
- Technical Assistant: Typical work: Assist with assembly, testing, inspection, laboratory equipment and technical production work; Typical study route (check each notice): Usually a relevant engineering diploma for the discipline listed in the notice.

chunks.source: ISRO Career Guide Jobs Exams Resources
chunks.heading: 1. Main ISRO job positions and job profiles
chunks.text:
- Technical Assistant: Typical work: Assist with assembly, testing, inspection, laboratory equipment and technical production work; Typical study route (check each notice): Usually a relevant engineering diploma for the discipline listed in the notice.
- Technician-B / Draughtsman: Typical work: Perform trade-based technical work, fabrication, fitting, electrical/electronics maintenance or technical drawings; Typical study route (check each notice): Usually SSLC/10th plus the prescribed ITI/NTC/NAC or other trade qualification listed in the notice.
- Scientific Assistant / Research Staff: Typical work: Support scientific laboratories, experiments, data analysis and research projects; Typical study route (check each notice): B.Sc. or a relevant postgraduate qualification, depending on the exact post.
- Administrative / Accounts / Purchase & Stores: Typical work: Manage office administration, budgets, accounts, procurement, contracts and personnel processes; Typical study route (check each notice): Degree and any required professional qualifications or experience stated in the notice.

chunks.source: ISRO Career Guide Jobs Exams Resources
chunks.heading: 1. Main ISRO job positions and job profiles
chunks.text:
- Administrative / Accounts / Purchase & Stores: Typical work: Manage office administration, budgets, accounts, procurement, contracts and personnel processes; Typical study route (check each notice): Degree and any required professional qualifications or experience stated in the notice.
- Medical / Specialist Staff: Typical work: Provide clinical care, occupational health and specialist services at eligible centres; Typical study route (check each notice): MBBS or the relevant recognised professional qualification and registration/specialisation, as required.
- Research Fellow (JRF/SRF), Research Associate, Project Scientist: Typical work: Work on a defined scientific or technical research project; many positions are project-specific or temporary; Typical study route (check each notice): Relevant postgraduate degree and/or GATE, NET or other criteria when specified by the individual advertisement.

chunks.source: ISRO Career Guide Jobs Exams Resources
chunks.heading: 2. Which degree should you choose?
chunks.text:
- Rocket and launch vehicle engineering: Class 11–12 Science with PCM → B.E./B.Tech Mechanical or Aerospace, or another accepted discipline.
- Satellite electronics and communications: PCM → B.E./B.Tech ECE, Electronics or an accepted equivalent.
- Space software, AI and data processing: PCM → B.E./B.Tech CSE, IT, AI/ML or another degree accepted for the target vacancy.
- Space science, astronomy or planetary research: B.Sc. → M.Sc. in Physics, Mathematics, Astronomy/Astrophysics or relevant field; Ph.D. for many research roles.
- Satellite imagery, GIS and Earth observation: Relevant bachelor's degree in engineering/science/geography/geology etc.; postgraduate study may be required for some posts.
- Technical Assistant: Relevant engineering diploma matching the vacancy.
- Technician-B: 10th/SSLC and the exact ITI/trade certificate specified.
- Administration / finance / purchase: Relevant bachelor's degree and any additional professional qualifications stated in the advertisement.
- Medical Officer: MBBS and prescribed registration or additional qualifications.

chunks.heading: 2. Which degree should you choose?
chunks.text: - Medical Officer: MBBS and prescribed registration or additional qualifications.

chunks.source: ISRO Career Guide Jobs Exams Resources
chunks.heading: 3. Is there a special exam to join ISRO?
chunks.text: There is no one common ISRO entrance exam for all jobs. ISRO's Centralised Recruitment Board (ICRB) and individual centres advertise different positions and may use different selection methods.

chunks.source: ISRO Career Guide Jobs Exams Resources
chunks.heading: 3. Is there a special exam to join ISRO? > A. Scientist/Engineer 'SC' — engineering graduates
chunks.text:
- Depending on the recruitment advertisement, selection may be through a written/computer-based test and interview, through GATE-score-based shortlisting and interview, or another method stated in that notice.
- Some recruitment drives combine different routes for different vacancies. Do not assume GATE is compulsory for every Scientist/Engineer post, and do not assume GATE alone guarantees selection.
- Prepare the core subjects for your engineering branch, engineering mathematics where relevant, and previous papers for the exact post/discipline.
- The official ICRB advertisement is the authority for accepted degrees, minimum marks, age, selection stages and dates.

chunks.source: ISRO Career Guide Jobs Exams Resources
chunks.heading: 3. Is there a special exam to join ISRO? > B. GATE — Graduate Aptitude Test in Engineering
chunks.text:
- Useful for engineering and some science-related recruitment routes when the specific ISRO notice accepts a GATE score.
- Choose the GATE paper that matches your discipline and the advertisement's requirements.
- Preparation: core undergraduate subjects, engineering mathematics where applicable, previous GATE papers, timed mock tests and error analysis.
- Official information: https://gate2026. iitg. ac. in/ (check the current year's official GATE website for the relevant cycle).

chunks.source: ISRO Career Guide Jobs Exams Resources
chunks.heading: 3. Is there a special exam to join ISRO? > C. Scientist / research fellowships and project posts
chunks.text:
- JRF, SRF, Research Associate and Project Scientist vacancies are advertised by centres such as SAC, NRSC, PRL, URSC and others.
- The criteria vary: some may ask for a relevant M.Sc./M.Tech, GATE, UGC-CSIR NET, another national test, research experience or an interview. Read the individual notice.
- For Physics, Mathematics and related research pathways, UGC-CSIR NET or GATE may be relevant to certain posts, but neither is a universal requirement for all ISRO research roles.

chunks.source: ISRO Career Guide Jobs Exams Resources
chunks.heading: 3. Is there a special exam to join ISRO? > D. Technical Assistant, Technician and other support roles
chunks.text:
- These roles generally have their own centre-specific recruitment notification and may use a written/computer-based test, trade/skill test or other prescribed assessment.
- Technical Assistant posts commonly require a relevant diploma; Technician-B commonly requires the specified ITI/trade qualification. The exact trade and marks requirements matter.
- Practise the technical syllabus, trade fundamentals, mathematics/reasoning if included, and the centre's official previous papers.

chunks.source: ISRO Career Guide Jobs Exams Resources
chunks.heading: 3. Is there a special exam to join ISRO? > E. Administrative, stenography, accounts and medical roles
chunks.text:
- Selection may include a computer-based/written examination, skill or typing test, interview, professional assessment or document verification, depending on the post.
- Medical roles require the professional qualification and registration listed in the advertisement; administrative and finance roles have their own qualification rules.

chunks.source: ISRO Career Guide Jobs Exams Resources
chunks.heading: 4. How to prepare for selection
chunks.text:
- Choose one target post and read its latest official advertisement from beginning to end.
- Confirm that your degree, branch, marks, age and any required experience match the eligibility criteria.
- Download the syllabus and official previous papers for that post/discipline.
- Build strong fundamentals in your degree subjects; practise numerical and conceptual questions rather than memorising solutions.
- Take timed mock tests and keep an error notebook with topics to revise.
- Prepare for the interview or skill test only if that stage is part of the stated selection process.
- Apply only through official recruitment links and beware of fake appointment letters or agents asking for money.

chunks.text:
- MOSDAC: How to use it: Meteorological and oceanographic satellite imagery and data for weather and Earth observation learning; Link: https://www. mosdac. gov. in/.

chunks.source: ISRO Career Guide Jobs Exams Resources
chunks.heading: 6. Subjects and books to prioritise
chunks.text:
- All engineering candidates: Mathematics and core subjects required by the specific branch; use your university's standard textbooks and official syllabus.
- Mechanical / Aerospace: Engineering mechanics, strength of materials, thermodynamics, fluid mechanics, heat transfer, propulsion-related basics, control and structures as applicable.
- Electronics / ECE: Network theory, analog/digital electronics, signals and systems, communication, control systems, electromagnetic fields and microprocessors as applicable.
- Computer Science / IT: Programming, data structures and algorithms, discrete mathematics, operating systems, databases, computer networks, software engineering and theory of computation as applicable.
- Physics / Space Science: Classical mechanics, electromagnetism, quantum mechanics, statistical mechanics, mathematical methods and the specialised subject listed for the exam.
- Remote Sensing / GIS: Remote sensing fundamentals, GIS, coordinate systems, image processing, geospatial analysis and interpretation of satellite data.

chunks.source: ISRO Career Guide Jobs Exams Resources
chunks.heading: 6. Subjects and books to prioritise
chunks.text:
- Remote Sensing / GIS: Remote sensing fundamentals, GIS, coordinate systems, image processing, geospatial analysis and interpretation of satellite data.
- Technical and ITI roles: Trade theory, workshop practice, safety, tools, measurements and the exact technical syllabus for the trade. Book selection note: use the books prescribed by your degree programme and standard references for your branch. The official syllabus and past papers should decide what to prioritise; avoid buying large sets of books before identifying the target exam.

chunks.source: ISRO Career Guide Jobs Exams Resources
chunks.heading: 7. A six-month foundation plan
chunks.text:
- Month 1: Review mathematics and fundamentals of the chosen discipline; read the target recruitment syllabus.
- Month 2: Cover the first major core subjects and practise topic-wise questions.
- Month 3: Continue core subjects and work through numerical and conceptual problems.
- Month 4: Finish high-priority topics and begin solving previous recruitment papers.
- Month 5: Take timed mock tests; analyse mistakes and revise weak areas.
- Month 6: Practise full papers, revise formulas and confirm the latest recruitment eligibility and selection method. Suggested daily routine: 1–2 hours of core subjects, 30 minutes of problem-solving and 15 minutes reviewing mistakes. Adapt this to your semester schedule and exam date.

chunks.source: ISRO Career Guide Jobs Exams Resources
chunks.heading: 8. Useful official links and verification
chunks.text:
- ISRO Careers: https://www. isro. gov. in/ISRO_EN/Careers. html
- Current Opportunities: https://www. isro. gov. in/CurrentOpportunities. html
- Official ISRO pages link to previous papers and the relevant detailed advertisements. Recruitment status and deadlines change, so check the live notice before applying.
- For example, ISRO recruitment notices in 2026 have included Scientist/Engineer recruitment, centre-specific technical roles, research/project positions and administrative posts. This illustrates why there is no single exam route for every job.

chunks.source: ISRO Career Guide Jobs Exams Resources
chunks.heading: 9. Your personal roadmap checklist
chunks.text:
- Current education: Class 10/12, diploma/ITI, B.E./B.Tech, B.Sc./M.Sc. or graduate.
- Branch or subject: CSE/IT, ECE, Mechanical, Electrical, Civil, Physics, Mathematics, Geography, etc.
- Preferred role: software/AI, rockets, satellite electronics, space science, remote sensing, technical work or administration.
- Target qualification and eligibility: confirm in the current vacancy advertisement.
- Exam route: GATE, ISRO written/CBT, interview, skill test, NET or other route only when specified.
- Resources: official syllabus, previous papers, core textbooks and free NPTEL/IIRS courses where relevant.

chunks.source: ISRO Career Guide Jobs Exams Resources
chunks.heading: Important disclaimer
chunks.text: This guide is for career planning, not a guarantee of eligibility or selection. Post names, accepted degrees, minimum marks, age limits, exam patterns and deadlines can change between recruitment cycles. Always follow the latest official advertisement for the exact vacancy. ISRO does not require candidates to pay agents for appointment.

To access data on MOSDAC: 1. Register for a user account at www. mosdac. gov. in. 2. Navigate to the "Data Services" section. 3. Select the desired satellite and product. 4. Choose temporal and spatial filters. 5. Download data in HDF or NetCDF format. Access to real-time products may require additional authorization.

Q: What is MOSDAC? A: MOSDAC (Meteorological and Oceanographic Satellite Data Archival Centre) is an ISRO portal for hosting weather, oceanographic, and climate data. Q: Is the data free to access? A: Yes, most data is freely accessible after registration. Q: Which satellites contribute data? A: INSAT-3D, INSAT-3DR, SCATSAT-1, Megha-Tropiques, Oceansat series. Q: What file formats are used? A: Data is available in HDF5, NetCDF, and GeoTIFF formats.

Geospatial Metadata: - AOI: Area of Interest (Lat, Long Bounding Box) - CRS: EPSG:4326 (WGS 84) - Resolution: 1km, 4km, 8km - Timezones: UTC for timestamp consistency - Tags: Cyclone, Precipitation, Monsoon, Ocean Current, Cloud Cover

INSAT-3D is an advanced meteorological satellite developed by ISRO. It monitors cyclones and cloud patterns. It carries a 6-channel imager and a 19-channel sounder. INSAT-3DR is the follow-up satellite to INSAT-3D. Both satellites are used for weather forecasting and disaster warning.
INSAT-3D is launched by PSLV. INSAT-3D monitors weather patterns. INSAT-3D carries an imager.

INSAT-3D is an advanced meteorological satellite developed by ISRO. It monitors cyclones and cloud patterns. It carries a 6-channel imager and a 19-channel sounder. INSAT-3D is launched by PSLV. INSAT-3D supports disaster warning systems. INSAT-3DR is the follow-up satellite to INSAT-3D. INSAT-3DR was launched by GSLV-F05.

MOSDAC (Meteorological and Oceanographic Satellite Data Archival Centre) is an initiative by ISRO to make satellite-based data accessible to the public and scientific community. The portal hosts a variety of data products including cloud coverage, temperature, humidity, precipitation, wind patterns, and ocean parameters. It also includes FAQs, documentation, and satellite mission details. The data is critical for researchers, policy makers, and weather monitoring agencies.

MOSDAC provides satellite-based meteorological and oceanographic products including: - Daily Rainfall Estimates (DRE) - Outgoing Longwave Radiation (OLR) - Cloud Motion Vectors (CMVs) - Sea Surface Temperature (SST) - Snow Cover Area (SCA) - Atmospheric Motion Vectors (AMVs) These products are derived from INSAT, SCATSAT-1, and Megha-Tropiques satellites.
INSAT-3D was launched by PSLV from Sriharikota. INSAT-3DR was launched aboard GSLV-F05. SCATSAT-1 provides ocean wind speed data. Megha-Tropiques focuses on tropical humidity and rainfall.

MOSDAC provides satellite-based meteorological and oceanographic data services to users across India. It includes real-time satellite imagery, rainfall estimates, sea surface temperature, and cyclone tracking information. The platform aggregates data from INSAT-3D, INSAT-3DR, SCATSAT-1, and other Indian satellites. These products support disaster management, weather forecasting, agriculture, and marine applications. Users can access data through interactive maps and download raw satellite data and processed products.

INSAT-3D and INSAT-3DR provide continuous weather monitoring from geostationary orbit. SCATSAT-1 measures wind speed and direction over oceans. Megha-Tropiques studies tropical humidity and precipitation. Oceansat-2 supports ocean color and surface wind data. These missions enhance India’s weather forecasting and climate research capabilities.
INSAT-3D carries meteorological payloads including an imager and a sounder. It observes temperature, humidity, and atmospheric pressure. The satellite helps forecast cyclones and thunderstorms.

chunks.source: Frequently asked questions about ISRO careers
chunks.heading: Is there one exam for all ISRO jobs?
chunks.text: There is no one common ISRO entrance exam for all jobs. ISRO's Centralised Recruitment Board (ICRB) and individual centres advertise different positions and may use different selection methods. Always read the official notice for the exact post.

chunks.source: Frequently asked questions about ISRO careers
chunks.heading: Can a diploma holder join ISRO?
chunks.text: Yes. Technical Assistant posts commonly require a relevant engineering diploma that matches the vacancy. Recruitment for Technical Assistants is usually centre-specific and may use a written or computer-based test, a trade or skill test, or another assessment. Check the official notice for the exact discipline, marks and age limit.

chunks.source: Frequently asked questions about ISRO careers
chunks.heading: Can I join ISRO after Class 12 or 10th?
chunks.text: After 10th or SSLC, the usual route in the guide is a trade qualification: Technician-B posts commonly require SSLC or 10th plus the specified ITI trade certificate. After Class 12, the guide's route for engineering roles is Class 11 and 12 Science with PCM followed by a B.E. or B.Tech, and for science roles a B.Sc. followed by an M.Sc. Scientist and Engineer posts need the degree named in the notice.

chunks.source: Frequently asked questions about ISRO careers
chunks.heading: Which degree is needed to become a scientist or engineer at ISRO?
chunks.text: For Scientist/Engineer posts the guide lists B.E. or B.Tech in the discipline of the vacancy, such as Mechanical or Aerospace, Electronics and Communication, or Computer Science and IT. Space science research usually follows a B.Sc. then an M.Sc. in Physics, Mathematics or Astronomy, with a Ph.D. for many research roles.

chunks.source: Frequently asked questions about ISRO careers
chunks.heading: Is GATE compulsory for ISRO?
chunks.text: Do not assume GATE is compulsory for every Scientist/Engineer post, and do not assume GATE alone guarantees selection. Some recruitment drives shortlist by GATE score and some use their own written test, so the official advertisement decides.

chunks.source: Frequently asked questions about ISRO careers
chunks.heading: Where do I apply for ISRO jobs?
chunks.text: Apply only through the official ISRO Careers page and the ISRO Current Opportunities page. Beware of fake appointment letters and of agents asking for money, because ISRO does not require candidates to pay agents for appointment.

chunks.source: Frequently asked questions about ISRO careers
chunks.heading: How do I start preparing for ISRO exams?
chunks.text: Choose one target post and read its latest official advertisement. Confirm your degree, marks and age match the eligibility. Download the syllabus and previous papers, build strong fundamentals in your degree subjects, take timed mock tests and keep an error notebook. The guide suggests about one to two hours of core subjects, 30 minutes of problem-solving and 15 minutes reviewing mistakes each day, and a six-month plan.

chunks.source: Frequently asked questions about ISRO careers
chunks.heading: Which books should I read for ISRO exams?
chunks.text: The guide names no specific books. It advises using the books prescribed by your degree programme and standard references for your branch, and letting the official syllabus and past papers decide what to prioritise. Avoid buying large sets of books before you know your target exam.

chunks.source: ISRO history and human spaceflight notes
chunks.heading: Founding of India's space programme
chunks.text: India's space programme began in the early 1960s under Dr Vikram Sarabhai, who believed that space technology should serve national development through communication, education, weather forecasting and resource mapping. In 1962 the government set up the Indian National Committee for Space Research (INCOSPAR) with Sarabhai as its chairman. The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) was formed on 15 August 1969, and the Department of Space and the Space Commission were created in 1972.

chunks.source: ISRO history and human spaceflight notes
chunks.heading: How the programme began with limited resources
chunks.text: The early programme had very little money, equipment or infrastructure, so it grew through small, inventive steps. The Thumba Equatorial Rocket Launching Station near Thiruvananthapuram was chosen in 1963 because the magnetic equator passes close by, which suits upper-atmosphere research. Its first offices and workshops were set up in a local church, the bishop's house and a cattle shed, and early rocket parts were carried by bicycle and bullock cart. The first sounding rocket was launched from Thumba on 21 November 1963. Young engineers were recruited and trained on the job, and the team built its own rockets and instruments step by step, starting with sounding rockets before moving on to satellite launch vehicles.

chunks.source: ISRO history and human spaceflight notes
chunks.heading: Early satellites and space for development
chunks.text: India's first satellite, Aryabhata, was built by ISRO and launched on 19 April 1975 on a Soviet rocket. Sarabhai had died in December 1971 and did not see it. The Satellite Instructional Television Experiment (SITE) of 1975 and 1976 used a borrowed NASA satellite to broadcast educational television to villages in several states, showing how space could reach rural communities. The Rohini, Bhaskara and APPLE satellites followed in the late 1970s and early 1980s, and the INSAT series, launched from 1982, built the national communication and weather network.

chunks.source: ISRO history and human spaceflight notes
chunks.heading: SLV-3, India's first satellite launch vehicle
chunks.text: SLV-3 (Satellite Launch Vehicle-3) was India's first experimental launch vehicle for satellites. It was a four-stage, all solid-propellant rocket about 22 metres tall, weighing about 17 tonnes at liftoff and able to place a payload of roughly 40 kg in low Earth orbit. Dr A. P. J. Abdul Kalam was the project director. It flew four times from Sriharikota. The first launch on 10 August 1979 failed. The second launch on 18 July 1980 placed the 35 kg Rohini RS-1 satellite in orbit. The third launch in 1981 reached a lower orbit than intended, and the fourth launch in 1983 succeeded. The 1980 success made India one of the few countries able to launch a satellite on its own rocket.

chunks.source: ISRO history and human spaceflight notes
chunks.heading: Engineering lessons commonly drawn from SLV-3
chunks.text: The control and guidance system must be tested exhaustively. The 1979 failure was traced to a fault in the second-stage control system and was studied in detail before the next launch. Failure analysis should be open and systematic. Data from every flight, including the failed one, drove design changes for the 1980 flight. Redundancy and strict quality checks matter, because one small valve or component failure can lose an entire vehicle. Building solid-propellant motors, stage separation, heat protection and closed-loop guidance in-house created the skills that later made the ASLV and PSLV possible. The SLV-3 first stage was also used in India's early Agni technology demonstrator. Integrating many specialist groups under one mission goal is a leadership skill in itself. As recounted in Kalam's memoir Wings of Fire, ISRO chairman Satish Dhawan publicly took responsibility for the 1979 failure and later let the project team face the press after the 1980 success.

chunks.source: ISRO history and human spaceflight notes
chunks.heading: Learning from a launch failure
chunks.text: Treat a failure as data, not as blame. Good practice drawn from ISRO's experience is to take responsibility as a leader, analyse the failure openly with the whole team, find and fix the root cause, test again before flying, and credit the team when things succeed. SLV-3 failed on its first flight in 1979 and succeeded in 1980. The first PSLV launch on 20 September 1993 did not reach orbit because of a control problem, and PSLV flew successfully in October 1994 and has since become a very reliable launcher. The Vikram lander of Chandrayaan-2 was lost during the final descent in September 2019. Chandrayaan-3 was then redesigned using a failure-based approach with sturdier landing sensors, more fuel and a larger landing area, and it landed successfully on 23 August 2023.

chunks.source: ISRO history and human spaceflight notes
chunks.heading: Prof. Satish Dhawan
chunks.text: Satish Dhawan (1920 to 2002) was an aerospace engineer known for his research on boundary layers in fluid flow. He directed the Indian Institute of Science in Bengaluru from 1962 to 1981 and chaired ISRO from 1972 to 1984. He is remembered for a leadership style that protected young engineers, accepted responsibility for failures and shared credit for successes. The Sriharikota launch centre was renamed the Satish Dhawan Space Centre after his death.

chunks.source: ISRO history and human spaceflight notes
chunks.heading: Dr. A. P. J. Abdul Kalam
chunks.text: A. P. J. Abdul Kalam (1931 to 2015) was born in Rameswaram, Tamil Nadu. He worked at ISRO, where he was project director of SLV-3, and later at DRDO on missile programmes including Agni and Prithvi. He served as Principal Scientific Adviser to the Government of India and as the 11th President of India from 2002 to 2007. He is known as the Missile Man of India and wrote the memoir Wings of Fire.

chunks.source: ISRO history and human spaceflight notes
chunks.heading: Dr. Vikram Sarabhai
chunks.text: Vikram Sarabhai (1919 to 1971) was born in Ahmedabad and was a physicist who studied cosmic rays. He founded the Physical Research Laboratory in 1947, led INCOSPAR from 1962, and is regarded as the father of the Indian space programme. He championed the use of satellites for education, communication and development. The Vikram lander of Chandrayaan-2 and Chandrayaan-3 is named after him.

chunks.source: ISRO history and human spaceflight notes
chunks.heading: Rakesh Sharma and India's first astronaut flight
chunks.text: Rakesh Sharma, an Indian Air Force pilot, became the first Indian to travel to space. He flew on the Soviet Soyuz T-11 spacecraft, launched on 3 April 1984, and spent about eight days in orbit, working aboard the Salyut 7 space station on science and Earth-observation experiments. When Prime Minister Indira Gandhi asked how India looked from space, he replied that it looked better than the rest of the world, echoing the song Saare Jahan Se Accha.

chunks.source: ISRO history and human spaceflight notes
chunks.heading: Gaganyaan, India's human spaceflight programme
chunks.text: The goal of Gaganyaan is to demonstrate India's ability to send a crew of up to three astronauts to low Earth orbit at about 400 km for up to three days and bring them home safely, landing in the sea near the Indian coast. It uses a human-rated version of the LVM3 rocket and an orbital module made of a crew module and a service module, with a crew escape system for safety. ISRO is building up to the crewed flight through uncrewed test flights, including one carrying the robotic humanoid Vyommitra. The Test Vehicle Abort Mission TV-D1 on 21 October 2023 demonstrated the crew escape system and recovery from the Bay of Bengal. Four Indian Air Force test pilots were named astronaut-designates in February 2024 and trained in Russia and at the Astronaut Training Facility in Bengaluru. One of them, Group Captain Shubhanshu Shukla, flew to the International Space Station on the private Axiom-4 mission in mid-2025. The date of the first crewed Gaganyaan flight has been revised several times, so check ISRO for the latest schedule.

chunks.source: ISRO history and human spaceflight notes
chunks.heading: Gaganyaan, India's human spaceflight programme
chunks.text: The date of the first crewed Gaganyaan flight has been revised several times, so check ISRO for the latest schedule. India has also announced longer-term goals of a national space station and a crewed Moon landing.

chunks.source: ISRO history and human spaceflight notes
chunks.heading: Chandrayaan-3: how it reached the Moon
chunks.text: Chandrayaan-3 launched on 14 July 2023 on an LVM3-M4 rocket from Sriharikota into an elliptical Earth orbit. Over the following weeks the propulsion module fired its engine several times to raise the orbit. On 1 August 2023 a trans-lunar injection burn sent it toward the Moon, and on 5 August 2023 it was captured by lunar gravity. Further burns lowered it to a circular orbit about 100 km above the Moon. The lander module, Vikram carrying the Pragyan rover, separated on 17 August 2023 and lowered its orbit to about 30 km by 100 km. Powered descent began from about 30 km altitude on 23 August 2023, and Vikram touched down near the lunar south pole at about 18:04 IST. Pragyan rolled out and worked for about one lunar day, roughly 14 Earth days. The landing site was named Shiv Shakti Point, and 23 August is now celebrated as National Space Day.

chunks.source: ISRO history and human spaceflight notes
chunks.heading: Chandrayaan-3 science results
chunks.text: Vikram carried instruments for lunar soil temperature (ChaSTE), plasma near the surface (RAMBHA-LP) and seismic activity (ILSA), plus a laser retroreflector. The Pragyan rover carried a laser-induced breakdown spectroscope and an alpha particle X-ray spectrometer. They confirmed sulphur and other elements in the lunar soil near the south pole, and ChaSTE recorded a steep temperature drop within the top few centimetres of soil.

chunks.source: ISRO history and human spaceflight notes
chunks.heading: Kalpana Chawla
chunks.text: Kalpana Chawla (1962 to 2003) was born in Karnal, Haryana, studied aerospace engineering and became a NASA astronaut. She was the first woman of Indian origin in space, flying on Space Shuttle Columbia mission STS-87 in November 1997 as a mission specialist and robotic arm operator. She died with her six crewmates when Columbia broke up on re-entry at the end of mission STS-107 on 1 February 2003. ISRO's Kalpana-1 weather satellite was named in her honour.

chunks.source: ISRO history and human spaceflight notes
chunks.heading: Sunita Williams
chunks.text: Sunita Williams was born in 1965 in Euclid, Ohio, to an Indian-American father. She is a retired US Navy captain and helicopter pilot who was selected as a NASA astronaut in 1998. She flew long missions to the International Space Station in 2006 to 2007 and 2012, commanding the station during Expedition 33. In June 2024 she launched on the first crewed flight of Boeing's Starliner for what was planned as a stay of about a week. Because of thruster and helium problems the capsule returned uncrewed, and she and Butch Wilmore stayed aboard for about nine months, coming home on a SpaceX Dragon in March 2025. She has completed nine spacewalks, holds the record for most spacewalking time by a woman, and has spent more than 600 days in space.

chunks.source: ISRO history and human spaceflight notes
chunks.heading: Daily life and teamwork aboard the International Space Station
chunks.text: The International Space Station orbits about 400 km above Earth at roughly 7.7 km per second, circling the planet about every 90 minutes, so the crew sees around 16 sunrises and sunsets a day. A typical crew is seven people from NASA, Roscosmos, ESA, JAXA and the Canadian Space Agency, and the station runs on UTC. A normal day includes science experiments, maintenance and repairs, conferences with ground teams, and about two hours of exercise on a treadmill, bike and resistance machine to protect muscles and bones in weightlessness. Astronauts sleep in small sleeping bags fixed to a wall and eat mostly packaged and rehydrated food, using tortillas instead of bread to avoid crumbs. Water is recycled, including from sweat and urine. Crews rely on clear communication, shared procedures and trust, because everyone depends on each other for repairs, spacewalks and emergencies. Meals together and video calls with family help keep morale high.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: Aditya-L1 ( Sanskrit : Āditya IPA: [aːd̪it̪jɐ] 'Sun', L1 ' Lagrange Point 1 ') is a coronagraphy spacecraft for studying the solar atmosphere , designed and developed by ISRO and various other Indian Space Research Institutes. It is orbiting at about 1.5 million km from Earth in a halo orbit around the Lagrange point 1 (L1) between the Earth and the Sun , where it will study the solar atmosphere, solar magnetic storms , and their impact on the environment around the Earth. It is the first Indian mission dedicated to observing the Sun. Nigar Shaji is the project's director. Aditya-L1 was launched aboard the PSLV-C57 at 11:50 IST on 2 September 2023. It successfully achieved its intended orbit nearly an hour later, and separated from its fourth stage at 12:57 IST. It was inserted at the L1 point on 6 January 2024, at 4:17 pm IST.

chunks.heading: Mission objectives
chunks.text:
The main objectives of Aditya-L1 are:
- To observe the dynamics of the solar chromosphere and corona :
- To study chromospheric and coronal heating , the physics of partially ionised plasma , of coronal mass ejections (CMEs) and their origins, of the coronal magnetic field and heat transfer mechanisms, and of flare exchanges.
- To observe the physical particle environment around its position.
- To determine the sequence of processes in multiple layers below the corona that lead to solar eruptions .
- To study space weather , and the origin, composition and dynamics of solar wind .
- To observe the in-situ particle and plasma environment providing data for the study of particle dynamics from the Sun.
- To study the factors affecting coronal and coronal loop plasma, such as temperature, velocity, and density.
- To analyse magnetic field topology and magnetic field measurements in the solar corona.

chunks.heading: Mission history > Development
chunks.text: Aditya-L1 in stowed configuration The mission was conceptualised in January 2008 by the Advisory Committee for Space Sciences (ADCOS). It was initially envisaged as a small, 400 kg (880 lb) satellite in a Low Earth Orbit (800 km) with a coronagraph to study the solar corona . An experimental budget of ₹3 crore was allocated for the financial year 2016–2017. The scope of the mission has since been expanded and it became a comprehensive solar and space environment observatory to be placed at Lagrange point 1 (L1), hence the mission was renamed as Aditya-L1. As of July 2019, the mission has an allocated cost of ₹378 crores , excluding launch costs. Aditya-L1 will provide observations of the Sun's photosphere , chromosphere and corona. Its scientific payloads must be placed outside the interference from the Earth's magnetic field and hence could not have been useful in the low Earth orbit, as proposed in the original mission concept back in 2008. One of the major unsolved problems in the field of solar physics is coronal heating.

chunks.heading: Mission history > Development
chunks.text: One of the major unsolved problems in the field of solar physics is coronal heating. The upper atmosphere of the Sun has a temperature of 2,000,000 K (2,000,000 °C; 3,600,000 °F), whereas the lower atmosphere is just 6,000 K (5,730 °C; 10,340 °F). In addition, it is not understood exactly how the Sun's radiation affects the dynamics of the Earth's atmosphere on a shorter as well as a longer time scale. The mission will obtain near-simultaneous images of the different layers of the Sun's atmosphere, which will reveal the ways in which energy is channeled and transferred from one layer to another. Thus, the mission will enable a comprehensive understanding of the dynamical processes of the Sun and address some of the outstanding problems in solar physics and heliophysics .

chunks.heading: Mission history > Launch
chunks.text: PSLV-C57 on launch pad housing Aditya-L1 Aditya L1 was mounted on a PSLV-XL carrier rocket with flight designation C57. The 44 meters tall rocket considered of four alternating solid fueled and liquid-fueled stages, along with 6 small solid rocket boosters. The combined rocket weighed in at about 321 tonnes. On 2 September 2023, at 11:50 IST , the Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV-C57) accomplished a successful launch of the Aditya-L1 It was inserted into a highly elliptical orbit around the earth with a perigee of 235 km and an apogee of 19500 km, inclined 19.2° to the earth. The spacecraft was launched from the Second Launch Pad of the Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC) located in Sriharikota at a launch Azimuth off 104°. Aditya-L1 , following a flight duration of 63 minutes and 20 seconds, achieved a successful injection into an elliptical orbit around the Earth at 12:54 IST. The launch was applauded by Dr Jitendra Singh Rana , India's Union minister for Science and Technology.

chunks.heading: Mission history > Orbit-raising burns
chunks.text: Trajectory of PSLV-C57/Aditya L1 Mission First orbit-raising burn On 3 September 2023, the Aditya-L1 performed its first Earth-bound maneuver, raising its orbit to a 245 km (152 mi) into 22,459 km (13,955 mi) orbit. Second orbit-raising burn On 5 September 2023, Aditya-L1 performed its second Earth-bound maneuver, raising its orbit to a 282 km (175 mi) into 40,225 km (24,995 mi) orbit. Third orbit-raising burn On 10 September 2023, Aditya-L1 performed its third Earth-bound maneuver, raising its orbit to a 296 km (184 mi) into 71,767 km (44,594 mi) orbit. Fourth orbit-raising burn On 15 September 2023, Aditya-L1 performed its fourth Earth-bound maneuver, raising its original orbit to a 256 km (159 mi) into 121,973 km (75,791 mi) orbit. This was the last of such maneuvers, being directly followed by the Trans-Lagrangian 1 Injection, which took place on 19 September. Trans-Lagrangian 1 Injection On 19 September 2023, Aditya-L1 performed its last maneuver around Earth to escape its orbit and headed towards the Lagrange 1 point, taking at least four months to further reach its destination, 1.5 million kilometers away.

chunks.heading: Mission history > Orbit-raising burns
chunks.text: On 19 September 2023, Aditya-L1 performed its last maneuver around Earth to escape its orbit and headed towards the Lagrange 1 point, taking at least four months to further reach its destination, 1.5 million kilometers away. On 30 September 2023, Aditya-L1 had escaped the Earth's sphere of influence and was on the way to the Lagrange point 1. During this journey a week before Orbital Insertion, the SUIT instrument captured an X-class solare flare and a CME on 31 December 2023. This was the first observations of a solar flare using near-UV light. Trajectory correction maneuver On 6 October 2023, Aditya-L1 performed a Trajectory Correction maneuvre (TCM1). It was needed to correct the trajectory evaluated after tracking the Trans-Lagrangian Point 1 Insertion (TL1I) maneuver performed on 19 September 2023.

chunks.heading: Mission history > Orbital Insertion
chunks.text: Lagrange points in the Sun–Earth system (not to scale) – a small object at any one of the five points will hold its relative position. Aditya-L1 underwent a series of four Earth-bound orbital maneuvres prior to its injection into a transfer orbit towards the Lagrange point (L1). It reached its designated orbit at the L1 point, which is about 1,500,000 km (930,000 mi) from Earth 126 days after its launch on 6 January 2024 at 4:17 IST. A small controlled firing of the spacecraft's liquid rocket engine was conducted to gently nudge it into an orbit around the L1 point. Aditya-L1 completed its first halo orbit around the L1 point on 2 July 2024. It takes it approximately 178 days to complete each orbit. It underwent two station-keeping maneuvers on 22 February and 7 June, and later one on 2 July. The European Space Operations Centre (ESOC), operated by the European Space Agency (ESA), supported the mission all through this phase. Its orbit is around 1% of the distance between the earth and the sun.

chunks.heading: Mission history > Orbital Insertion
chunks.text: Its orbit is around 1% of the distance between the earth and the sun. The spacecraft is planned to remain in its present halo orbit for the entire mission duration while being maintained at a stationkeeping Δv of 0.2–4 m/s per year.

chunks.heading: Payloads
chunks.text: The Aditya spacecraft before integration with the PSLV rocket The instruments of Aditya-L1 are tuned to observe the solar atmosphere, mainly the chromosphere and corona. In-situ instruments will observe the local environment at the L1 point. There are seven payloads on board, with four for remote sensing of the Sun and three for in-situ observation. The payloads have been developed by different laboratories in India with the close collaborations of various ISRO centers. The 1,500 kg (3,300 lb) satellite carries seven scientific payloads, including instruments to measure and monitor coronal heating , solar wind acceleration, coronal magnetometry, the origin of near-UV solar radiation (which drives Earth's upper atmospheric dynamics and global climate), the coupling of the solar photosphere to the chromosphere and corona, and in-situ characterisations of the space environment around Earth by measuring energetic particle fluxes and magnetic fields of the solar wind, and solar magnetic storms.

chunks.heading: Payloads > Visible Emission Line Coronagraph (VELC)
chunks.text: The Visible Emission Line Coronagraph (VELC) is a primary payload aboard on the Aditya spacecraft . The VELC is an internally occulted reflective coronagraph designed to fulfil specific observation needs. The instrument allows for high spatial resolution imaging 1.25-2.5 arcseconds of the Sun's corona, simultaneous observations in three modes (Imaging, Spectroscopy and Spectro-polarimetry ), and even utilizes artificial intelligence to aid in the detection of coronal mass ejections (CMEs). The instrument was developed by Indian Institute of Astrophysics , Bengaluru .

chunks.heading: Payloads > Solar Ultraviolet Imaging Telescope (SUIT)
chunks.text: The SUIT is an ultraviolet imaging telescope designed to study the solar spectral radiation in the ultraviolet range. It operates within the wavelength range of 200–400 nm, using both narrowband and broadband filters. The SUIT utilises 11 different filters. The filters have been selected carefully to ensure coverage of the lower (photosphere) and middle (chromosphere) atmosphere of the Sun, the first approach of its kind in such observations. The SUIT provides near-simultaneous coverage of the solar atmosphere, from lower photosphere to the upper chromosphere. The instrument was developed by Inter University Centre for Astronomy & Astrophysics , Pune , in collaboration with ISRO.

chunks.heading: Payloads > Solar Low Energy X-ray Spectrometer (SoLEXS)
chunks.text: The SoLEXS is an X-ray spectrometer designed to continuously measure the solar soft X-ray flux (2 keV-22 keV) from the Sun-Earth Lagrangian point L1. These measurements can be used to better understand the properties of the Sun's corona, in particular, why the temperature of the corona is so high. The SoLEXS will observe solar flares, and in conjunction with data provided by the VELC, will help study the complex thermal properties of the Sun's outer layers. The instrument was developed by U. R. Rao Satellite Centre , Bengaluru.

chunks.heading: Payloads > High Energy L-1 Orbiting X-ray Spectrometer (HEL1OS)
chunks.text: Developed by the Space Astronomy Group, URSC, the HEL1OS (pronounced helios) is an x-ray spectrometer designed to study solar flares in the x-ray spectrum, in particular, energy bands of 10-150 Kev ( kilo-electron volts ). Using a twin-pair of Cadmium Telluride (CdTe) and Cadmium Zinc Telluride (CZT) detectors, the instrument aims to study the acceleration and movement of electrons in the Sun's corona, as well as to study the cut-off energy between thermal and non-thermal solar emissions.

chunks.heading: Payloads > Aditya Solar Wind Particle Experiment (ASPEX)
chunks.text: The ASPEX is an instrument composed of low and high energy particle spectrometers, designed to conduct measurements of the Sun's solar wind particles. Solar Wind Ion Spectrometer (SWIS), the low energy spectrometer, contains two analysers, each designed to study particles entering the device in different planes. Supra Thermal Energetic Particle Spectrometer (STEPS), the high energy spectrometer, also consists of two parts, STEPS 1 and STEPS 2, both designed to separate protons and alpha particles and measure the integrated flux . The instrument was developed by the Physical Research Laboratory , Ahmedabad .

chunks.heading: Payloads > Plasma Analyser Package for Aditya (PAPA)
chunks.text: The PAPA is an instrument on board the Aditya-L1 designed to study the temperature, distribution and velocity of the solar winds. The instrument contains two sensors; the Solar Wind Electron Energy Probe (SWEEP) and the Solar Wind lon Composition Analyser (SWICAR). The detectors are used in conjunction to analyse the energy levels of electrons and ions within the solar wind. The instrument was developed by the Space Physics Laboratory of the Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre , Thiruvananthapuram .

chunks.heading: Payloads > Digital Magnetometers
chunks.text: On board the Aditya-L1 spacecraft are a pair of magnetic sensors on a deployable boom, one positioned in the middle and the other at the tip. The purpose of these sensors is to gather information about the magnitude and direction of the Interplanetary Magnetic Fields (IMF), as well as to study other events such as Coronal Mass Ejections (CME). Data from the magnetic sensors will be used to supplement that of the PAPA and ASPEX sensors.

chunks.heading: Science phase
chunks.text: Following commissioning and checkout, Adiya L1 began Science observations about three months into the mission.

chunks.heading: Science phase > 2024
chunks.text: The PAPA instrument on the spacecraft was operationalised on 12 December 2023, and made its first observation on 10 and 11 February 2024 using the PAPA instrument to observe the Sun from its vantage point–a distance of about 1 million miles (1.5 million kilometers). Post-launch calibration of SUIT has now characterised its filters in detail. In-orbit testing of the transmission, spatial variation, and out-of-band performance confirmed that most filters meet design expectations, with only a few showing slightly higher out-of-band transmission than predicted (still below 1%). Additionally, on 31 December 2023, SUIT observed a plasma blob ejection from the Sun moving at speeds up to 1500 km/s, the highest recorded by the mission thus far. On 11 January 2024, upon reaching its orbit, ISRO successfully deployed a 6-meter magnetometer boom aboard the Aditya-L1 in the Halo orbit at the Lagrange Point L1. After the liftoff, the boom had been stowed for 132 days. The in-orbit deployment period that was measured was roughly 9 seconds, which is well within the 8–12 second prediction range.

chunks.heading: Science phase > 2024
chunks.text: The in-orbit deployment period that was measured was roughly 9 seconds, which is well within the 8–12 second prediction range. The magnetometer boom will measure the low-intensity interplanetary magnetic field in space using two high-accuracy fluxgate magnetometer sensors that are carried aboard. In order to reduce the impact of the spacecraft's magnetic field on measurements, the sensors are placed 3 and 6 meters away from the craft. Using a dual sensor system also helps to cancel out the spacecraft's magnetic influence and facilitates accurate estimation. Carbon-fiber-reinforced polymers (CFRP) were used in the construction of the boom segments. Through the use of spring-driven hinge mechanisms, the five pieces are joined to enable folding in close proximity to the craft throughout the journey and opening up upon reaching the desired orbit. The hinges lock into place as the mechanism fans out. In the stowed position, two hold-downs firmly secure the boom in place. Information obtained via the telemetry switches validates the release of the hold-down, the initial motion, and the locking of every hinge.

chunks.heading: Science phase > 2024
chunks.text: Information obtained via the telemetry switches validates the release of the hold-down, the initial motion, and the locking of every hinge. In conjunction with the Udaipur Solar Observatory and research stations at Thumba , ISRO mobilised all its observation platforms and systems to record the signatures of a Massive Solar Flare in May 2024. Aditya-L1, Chandrayaan-2 's orbiter and XPoSat have made observations and observed signatures have been analysed. Aditya-L1 used ASPEX, SOLEX, HEL1OS and its magnetometer instruments to record data. This storm, called " Gannon's Storm " was the strongest solar storm recorded since the beginning of the 21st Century. Using the Magneometers on Aditya L1 and other NASA spacecraft discovered that two distinct CMEs collided in space such that the magnetic field lines inside one of them snapped and rejoined in new ways, a process called magnetic reconnection . This sudden reversal of the magnetic field made the storm's impact much stronger than expected. Using observations of particles and fields measurements from Aditya-L1, and combining it with other ground based measurements as well as the GOES-18 spacecraft, unusual dawn-side magnetic disturbances observed during this storm were most likely caused by a rare type of space current normally confined to auroral regions of the Sun.

chunks.heading: Science phase > 2024
chunks.text: During very strong storms, when the Earth's magnetosphere becomes highly compressed, such rare auroral current systems ingress into lower solar latitudes, extending much farther towards the mean solar equator. Ground based observations from the Gauribidanur radio telescope and IIA astronomers using VELC detected multiple CME-driven shock waves forming at a distance of approximately 130,000 kilometers above the Sun's surface and traveling at nearly 1,700 kilometers per second on 27 May 2024. This is the closest distance from the Sun at which such a shock and its associated radio burst have been unambiguously detected. On 16 July 2024, the VELC instrument was used to measure another large Coronal Mass ejection from the Sun. It also studied an accompanying solar flare and the motion of solar particles within the Sun. Global Solar wind impact map from 2024 Aditya L1 data Global Solar wind impact map from 2024 Aditya L1 data

chunks.heading: Science phase > 2025
chunks.text: Marking its first year of science observation, ISRO released the maiden set of the scientific data from the Aditya L1 to the global scientific community on 6 January 2025, at the ISRO Headquarters in Bengaluru. ISRO presented the second set on 14 February 2025. On 22 February 2024, Aditya L1 captured the first-ever image of a X6.3-class solar flare ‘kernel’ occurring in the photosphere and the chromosphere . The image was taken alongside operations of SUIT, SoLEXS and HEL1OS instruments in the Near-Ultraviolet band. Further studies of a continuation event in October 2024 decoded the impact of Solar winds with the Earth's Magnectic field and the result of these interactions that affected Geostationary satellites in earth orbit. The study also noted that currents over high latitude regions intensified, potentially heating the Earth's upper atmosphere and causing enhanced atmospheric escape . Scientists from IIA also reported observations of a flareless coronal mass ejection from reading taken by VELC in March 2025.

chunks.heading: Science phase > 2025
chunks.text: Scientists from IIA also reported observations of a flareless coronal mass ejection from reading taken by VELC in March 2025. Observations from the onboard MAG payload show that during solar transient events in 2024, the interplanetary magnetic field magnitude increased above typical quiet-solar levels, and the spectral slope of turbulence approached a Kolmogorov -5/3 kind of behaviour. To verify changes in spectral behaviour, the data was compared with that from a day when quiet solar winds were present, resulting in a strong contrast. The quiet periods exhibit anisotropic turbulence, whereas the behaviour from the event exhibited quasi-isotropic behaviour, with spectral slopes closely following the Kolmogorov spectrum across all three IMF components. A Workshop was conducted based on these findings in October, with the spacecraft releasing over 20TB of data. In 2025, using the data from the VELC instrument, researchers from IIA and NASA created the very first spectroscopic observations of a CME in the visible wavelength range.

chunks.heading: Science phase > 2025
chunks.text: In 2025, using the data from the VELC instrument, researchers from IIA and NASA created the very first spectroscopic observations of a CME in the visible wavelength range. They also estimated the electron density, energy, mass, temperature and speed of a CME very close to the Sun.

chunks.heading: Science phase > 2026
chunks.text: On the second anniversary (6 January 2026) of Aditya-L1's launch, ISRO made an Announcement of Opportunity to solicit proposals for scientific research data from its first AO cycle observations. ISRO and ESA conducted a workshop at IIST in Thiruvanthapuram between 19 and 23 January 2026 presenting data from Aditya-L1, Proba-3 and Solar Orbiter presenting complementary vantage data points from each mission. The 2026 Indian budget also proposed to rebuild the National Large Solar Telescope at a cost of about ₹1,000 crore (US$100 million) by 2030 for it to serve as a complement to solar data from Aditya-L1. Over 27 Terabytes of information have been received from Aditya-L1 by April 2026 and were published. ISRO also made the call for the Second cycle of its AOC to disseminate data from the Aditya-L1 spacecraft. This will allow researchers to use the Instruments on Aditya-L1 to conduct independent research and experiments. Aditya L1 also presented the first comprehensive analysis of photospheric iron fluorescence .

chunks.heading: Science phase > 2026
chunks.text: Aditya L1 also presented the first comprehensive analysis of photospheric iron fluorescence . The "iron fluorescence" phenomenon was observed during 47 massive X-class solar flares in the from the year 2024. It is caused when a small fraction of the Sun's massive burst of high-energy X-rays during solar flare events fall back on the cooler solar photosphere, causing it to interact with the abundant neutral iron atoms that then absorbs the energy to emit their own X-ray glow around an energy level of 6.40 keV. The spacecraft used the SoLEXS instrument for this analysis. ISRO released the call for the third observation cycle to scientists for observation time during the third survey phase in July 2026.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: AstroSat is India's first dedicated multi-wavelength space telescope . It was launched on a PSLV-XL on 28 September 2015. With the success of this satellite, ISRO has proposed launching AstroSat-2 as a successor for AstroSat .

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: After the success of the satellite-borne Indian X-ray Astronomy Experiment (IXAE), which was launched in 1996, the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) approved further development for a full-fledged astronomy satellite, AstroSat , in 2004. A number of astronomy research institutions in India, and abroad have jointly built instruments for the satellite. Important areas requiring coverage include studies of astrophysical objects ranging from nearby Solar System objects to distant stars and objects at cosmological distances; timing studies of variables ranging from pulsations of hot white dwarfs to those of active galactic nuclei can be conducted with AstroSat as well, with time scales ranging from milliseconds to days. AstroSat is a multi- wavelength astronomy mission on an IRS-class satellite into a near-Earth, equatorial orbit . The five instruments on board cover the visible (320–530 nm), near UV (180–300 nm), far UV (130–180 nm), soft X-ray (0.3–8 keV and 2–10 keV) and hard X-ray (3–80 keV and 10–150 keV) regions of the electromagnetic spectrum .

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: The five instruments on board cover the visible (320–530 nm), near UV (180–300 nm), far UV (130–180 nm), soft X-ray (0.3–8 keV and 2–10 keV) and hard X-ray (3–80 keV and 10–150 keV) regions of the electromagnetic spectrum . The sanctioned cost of Astrosat was ₹177.85 crore (equivalent to about 20 million USD as of March 2025). Astrosat was successfully launched on 28 September 2015 from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre on board a PSLV-XL vehicle at 10:00AM.

chunks.heading: Mission
chunks.text:
Artist's conception of a binary star system with one black hole and one main sequence star Tilted view of Astrosat AstroSat is a proposal-driven general purpose observatory, with main scientific focus on:
- Simultaneous multi-wavelength monitoring of intensity variations in a broad range of cosmic sources
- Monitoring the X-ray sky for new transients
- Sky surveys in the hard X-ray and UV bands
- Broadband spectroscopic studies of X-ray binaries, AGN , SNRs , clusters of galaxies, and stellar coronae
- Studies of periodic and non-periodic variability of X-ray sources AstroSat performs multi-wavelength observations covering spectral bands from radio, optical, IR, UV, and X-ray wavelengths. Both individual studies of specific sources of interest and surveys are undertaken. While radio, optical, and IR observations would be coordinated through ground-based telescopes, the high energy regions, i.e., UV, X-ray and visible wavelength, would be covered by the dedicated satellite-borne instrumentation of AstroSat .

chunks.heading: Mission
chunks.text:
While radio, optical, and IR observations would be coordinated through ground-based telescopes, the high energy regions, i.e., UV, X-ray and visible wavelength, would be covered by the dedicated satellite-borne instrumentation of AstroSat . The mission would also study near simultaneous multi-wavelength data from different variable sources. In a binary system , for example, regions near the compact object emit predominantly in the X-ray , with the accretion disc emitting most of its light in the UV/optical waveband, whereas the mass of the donating star is brightest in the optical band. The observatory will also carry out:
- Low- to moderate-resolution spectroscopy over a wide energy band with the primary emphasis on studies of X-ray-emitting objects
- Timing studies of periodic and aperiodic phenomena in X-ray binaries
- Studies of pulsations in X-ray pulsars
- Quasi-periodic oscillations , flickering, flaring, and other variations in X-ray binaries
- Short- and long-term intensity variations in active galactic nuclei

chunks.heading: Mission
chunks.text:
- Short- and long-term intensity variations in active galactic nuclei
- Time-lag studies in low/hard X-rays and UV/optical radiation
- Detection and study of X-ray transients. In particular, the mission will train its instruments at active galactic nuclei, which are believed to contain super-massive black holes.

chunks.heading: Payloads
chunks.text:
The scientific payload contains six instruments.
- The Ultra Violet Imaging Telescope (UVIT) performs imaging simultaneously in three channels: 130–180 nm, 180–300 nm, and 320–530 nm. The three detectors are vacuum image intensifiers manufactured by Photek, UK . The FUV detector consists of a CsI photocathode with a MgF 2 input optic, the NUV detector consists of CsTe photocathode with a fused-silica input optic and the visible detector consists of an alkali-antimonide photocathode with a fused-silica input optic. The field of view is a circle of ~28′ diameter and the angular resolution is 1.8" for the ultraviolet channels and 2.5″ for the visible channel. In each of the three channels a spectral band can be selected through a set of filters mounted on a wheel; in addition, for the two ultraviolet channels a grating can be selected in the wheel to do slitless spectroscopy with a resolution of ~100. The primary mirror diameter of the telescope is 40 cm.
- The Soft X-ray imaging Telescope (SXT) employs focusing optics and a deep depletion CCD camera at the focal plane to perform X-ray imaging in the 0.3–8.0 keV band.

chunks.heading: Payloads
chunks.text:
- The Soft X-ray imaging Telescope (SXT) employs focusing optics and a deep depletion CCD camera at the focal plane to perform X-ray imaging in the 0.3–8.0 keV band. The optics will consist of 41 concentric shells of gold-coated conical foil mirrors in an approximate Wolter-I configuration (the effective area of 120 cm 2 ). The focal plane CCD camera will be very similar to that flown on SWIFT XRT. The CCD will be operated at a temperature of about −80 °C by thermoelectric cooling.
- The Large Area X-ray Proportional Counter (LAXPC) covers X-ray timing and low-resolution spectral studies over a broad energy band (3–80 keV), Astrosat will use a cluster of 3 co-aligned identical Large Area X-ray Proportional Counters (LAXPCs), each with a multi-wire-multi-layer configuration and a Field of View of 1° × 1°. These detectors are designed to achieve (I) wide energy band of 3–80 keV, (II) high detection efficiency over the entire energy band, (III) narrow field of view to minimize source confusion, (IV) moderate energy resolution , (V) small internal background and (VI) long lifetime in space.

chunks.heading: Payloads
chunks.text:
These detectors are designed to achieve (I) wide energy band of 3–80 keV, (II) high detection efficiency over the entire energy band, (III) narrow field of view to minimize source confusion, (IV) moderate energy resolution , (V) small internal background and (VI) long lifetime in space. The effective area of the telescope is 6000 cm 2 .
- The Cadmium Zinc Telluride Imager (CZTI) is a hard X-ray imager. It will consist of a Pixellated Cadmium-Zinc-Telluride detector array of 500 cm 2 effective area and the energy range from 10 to 150 kev. The detectors have a detection efficiency close to 100% up to 100 keV, and have a superior energy resolution (~2% at 60 keV) compared to scintillation and proportional counters. Their small pixel size also facilitates medium resolution imaging in hard x-rays. The CZTI will be fitted with a two dimensional coded mask , for imaging purposes. The sky brightness distribution will be obtained by applying a deconvolution procedure to the shadow pattern of the coded mask recorded by the detector.

chunks.heading: Payloads
chunks.text:
The sky brightness distribution will be obtained by applying a deconvolution procedure to the shadow pattern of the coded mask recorded by the detector. Apart from spectroscopic studies, CZTI would be able to do sensitive polarization measurements for bright galactic X-ray sources in 100–300 keV.
- The Scanning Sky Monitor (SSM) consists of three position sensitive proportional counters, each with a one-dimensional coded mask, very similar in design to the All Sky Monitor on NASA's RXTE satellite . The gas-filled proportional counter will have resistive wires as anodes. The ratio of the output charge on either ends of the wire will provide the position of the X-ray interaction, providing an imaging plane at the detector. The coded mask, consisting of a series of slits, will cast a shadow on the detector, from which the sky brightness distribution will be derived.
- The Charged Particle Monitor (CPM) will be included as a part of Astrosat payloads to control the operation of the LAXPC, SXT and SSM.

chunks.heading: Payloads
chunks.text: - The Charged Particle Monitor (CPM) will be included as a part of Astrosat payloads to control the operation of the LAXPC, SXT and SSM. Even though the orbital inclination of the satellite will be 8 deg or less, in about 2/3 of the orbits, the satellite will spend a considerable time (15–20 minutes) in the South Atlantic Anomaly (SAA) region which has high fluxes of low energy protons and electrons. The high voltage will be lowered or put off using data from CPM when the satellite enters the SAA region to prevent damage to the detectors as well as to minimize ageing effect in the Proportional Counters.

chunks.heading: Ground support
chunks.text: The Ground Command and Control Center for Astrosat is the ISRO Telemetry, Tracking and Command Network (ISTRAC) at Bangalore, India. Command and control of the spacecraft, and scientific data downloads is possible during every visible pass over Bangalore. 10 out of 14 orbits per day are visible to the ground station. The satellite is capable of gathering 420 gigabits of data every day that can be downloaded during the 10 visible orbits by the Tracking and Data receiving center of ISRO in Bangalore. A third 11-meter antenna at the Indian Deep Space Network (IDSN) became operational in July 2009 to track Astrosat .

chunks.heading: AstroSat support cell
chunks.text: ISRO has set up a support cell for AstroSat at IUCAA , Pune . A MoU was signed between ISRO and IUCAA in May 2016. The support cell has been set up to give opportunity to the scientific community in making proposals on processing and usage of AstroSat data. The support cell will provide necessary resource materials, tools, training and help to the guest observers.

chunks.heading: Results
chunks.text: A gamma-ray burst was detected by Astrosat on 5 January 2017. There was a confusion whether this event was related to the gravitational wave signal detected by LIGO from the black hole merger event GW170104 on 4 January 2017. Astrosat helped in distinguishing between the two events. The gamma-ray burst from 4 January 2017 was identified as a distinct supernova explosion that would form a black hole. Astrosat also captured the rare phenomenon of a 6 billion year old small star or blue straggler feeding off and sucking out the mass and energy of a bigger companion star. On 31 May 2017, Astrosat , Chandra X-ray Observatory and Hubble Space Telescope simultaneously detected a coronal explosion on the nearest planet-hosting star Proxima Centauri On 6 November 2017 Nature Astronomy published a paper from Indian astronomers measuring the variations of X-ray polarisation of the Crab Pulsar in the Taurus constellation. This study was a project conducted by scientists from Tata Institute of Fundamental Research , Mumbai; the Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre , Thiruvananthapuram; ISRO Satellite Centre Bengaluru; the Inter-University Centre for Astronomy and Astrophysics , Pune; and the Physical Research Laboratory , Ahmedabad.

chunks.heading: Results
chunks.text: In July 2018, Astrosat has captured an image of a special galaxy cluster that is more than 800 million light years away from Earth. Named abell 2256 the galaxy cluster is made of three separate cluster of galaxy that are all merging with one another to eventually form a single massive cluster in the future. The three massive cluster contain more than 500 galaxies and the cluster is almost 100 times larger and more than 1500 times massive as our own galaxy. On 26 September 2018, the archival data of AstroSat was publicly released. As of 28 September 2018, data from AstroSat has been cited in around 100 publications in refereed journals. This figure is expected to rise after the public release of data from AstroSat. In 2019 AstroSat observed a very rare X-ray outburst in a Be/X-ray binary system RX J0209.6-7427. Only a couple of rare outbursts have been observed from this source hosting a neutron star. The last outburst was detected in 2019 after about 26 years. The accreting neutron star in this Be/X-ray binary system was found to be an ultraluminous X-ray Pulsar (ULXP) making it the second closest ULXP and the first ULXP in our neighbouring Galaxy in the Magellanic Clouds .

chunks.heading: Results
chunks.text:
The accreting neutron star in this Be/X-ray binary system was found to be an ultraluminous X-ray Pulsar (ULXP) making it the second closest ULXP and the first ULXP in our neighbouring Galaxy in the Magellanic Clouds . This source is the first ULX pulsar discovered with the AstroSat mission and only the eight known ULX pulsar. In August 2020, AstroSat had detected extreme-UV light from a galaxy located 9.3 billion light-years away from Earth. The galaxy called AUDFs01 was discovered by a team of Astronomers led by Kanak Saha from the Inter-University Centre for Astronomy and Astrophysics , Pune. In August 2025, researchers from ISRO, Haifa University , URSC & IIT-Guwahati observed the origins of X-ray flickering on a black hole named GRS 1915+105 and discovered that it's X-ray brightness alternated between bright and dim phases, each lasting several hundred seconds. This discovery will provide critical insights into how black holes interact with surrounding matter and release energy.

INTRODUCTION: Satellite measurements of ocean colour allow synoptic coverage of ocean biological production on a global scale. Satellite derived chlorophyll measurements provide global distribution of phytoplankton CHLa on high spatial and temporal scale. The accurate measurements of ocean chlorophyll concentration are very critical to understand the regional and global impact of climate change on marine ecosystem. Considering the contribution of chlorophyll-a measurements to the characterization of Earth’s climate, World Meteorological Organization (WMO) has identified CHL-a as one of the Essential Climate Variable (ECV) under ocean category.

Considering the contribution of chlorophyll-a measurements to the characterization of Earth’s climate, World Meteorological Organization (WMO) has identified CHL-a as one of the Essential Climate Variable (ECV) under ocean category. However, the continuous availability of satellite based CHL-a is a major challenge due to the obstruction of the visible part of the e. m spectrum by clouds. Moreover, the observations from ocean colour near coastal region suffer from inaccurate atmospheric correction due to the optical complexity in the coastal waters. Coupled physical-biogeochemical modelling provides a key insight into the interaction of elements in the physical and biogeochemical system of marine ecosystem. The coupled models, thus become an essential tool in the scientific community to elucidate the mechanism of physical and marine system and

predict its evolution in both space and time scale. It enhanced the scope to study the biogeochemical and ecological responses to physical forcing, which is a key component in the climate change science and environmental risk assessment. 2.1 Overview and Background: The synergistic use of satellite derived chlorophyll and model simulated chlorophyll is adapted in order to explore the advantages offered by both systems in the generation of analysed fields of chlorophyll. For this purpose, daily fields of model chlorophyll from a coupled physical-biogeochemical model are modified with respect to satellite derived chlorophyll data by statistically combining both fields of chlorophyll using Particle filter technique for the global ocean. Particle Filter is an ensemble based technique like ensemble Kalman filter (van Leeuwen, 2009). But unlike methods like EnKF, ensemble optimal interpolation (Evensen, 2003) etc, particle filter doesn’t change the dynamical balance of the system and also does not consider the apriori assumption of the Gaussianity of the probability distribution function (PDF) of the system.

But unlike methods like EnKF, ensemble optimal interpolation (Evensen, 2003) etc, particle filter doesn’t change the dynamical balance of the system and also does not consider the apriori assumption of the Gaussianity of the probability distribution function (PDF) of the system. This makes particle filter more suitable for non-linear systems like ocean dynamics. Recently the particle filter techniques have been successfully utilized in assimilation of chlorophyll data in a coupled bio-physical model (Ratheesh et al. , 2016) and in the assimilation of highly non-linear coastal waves in a wave models (Bhowmick et al. , 2019). 2.2 Objective The main objective of this document is to provide step wise implementation of the algorithm, along with required inputs and desired outputs. This document will form the basis of operational implementation of the algorithm. 2.3 Input data sets 2.3.1 Satellite Data: Chlorophyll-a global product from OCM3 onboard OCEANSAT-3 is used in the algorithm to improve model simulations of chlorophyll.

GAC products are available scene wise at 1 km resolution wise (https://bhoonidhi. nrsc. gov. in). More than 200 scenes are available daily for the entire globe. Therefore, a gridded field of OCM-3 chlorophyll-a is generated as an intermediate product for the global ocean at 4km resolution combining all the OCM-3 products available for the particular day.

2.3.2 Model Data: Chlorophyll from coupled physical-biogeochemical model (MOM5-TOPAZ) for the global ocean is used as the background chlorophyll field in the algorithm. This model is operationally running at SAC. 2.3.2.1 General description of the Ocean General Circulation Model Ocean General circulation model used for the simulation of physical parameters of ocean is Modular Ocean Model, version 5 (MOM-5). It is a numerical representation of the ocean’s hydrostatic primitive equations employing either Boussinesq (volume conserving) or non-Boussinesq (mass conserving) kinematics. The present study use Boussinesq kinematics. This model is developed by NOAA’s Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory (GFDL) in Princeton, USA. The horizontal grids used in MOM5 are generalized horizontal coordinates, with the coordinates assumed to be locally orthogonal. For global ocean climate modeling, MOM uses the tripolar grid that has a bipolar Arctic region (Murray , 1996). The model also employs a split-explicit time stepping scheme where fast two-dimensional dynamics is sub-cycled within the slower three dimensional dynamics.

The model also employs a split-explicit time stepping scheme where fast two-dimensional dynamics is sub-cycled within the slower three dimensional dynamics. MOM gives a wide array of vertical mixing schemes and the present model configuration used KPP scheme. 2.3.2.2. Description of the Ecosystem model The present configuration for global ocean is a coupled one, in which MOM5, the ocean component is coupled to an ocean ecosystem model. A comprehensive model of oceanic ecosystems and biogeochemical cycles is used to understand and simulate the ocean ecosystem. The model used is Tracers Of Phytoplankton and Allometric Zooplankton (TOPAZ). TOPAZ is a state of the art model that considers 22 tracers including three phytoplankton groups, two forms of dissolved organic matter, heterotrophic biomass, and dissolved inorganic species for C, N, P, Si, Fe, CaCO3 and O2 cycling. The model includes such processes as gas exchange, atmospheric deposition, scavenging, N2 fixation and water column and sediment denitrification, and runoff of C, N, Fe, O2, alkalinity and lithogenic material.

The model includes such processes as gas exchange, atmospheric deposition, scavenging, N2 fixation and water column and sediment denitrification, and runoff of C, N, Fe, O2, alkalinity and lithogenic material. The phytoplankton functional groups undergo co-limitation by light, nitrogen, phosphorus and iron with flexible physiology. Loss of phytoplankton is parameterized through

the size-based relationship of Dunne et al. (2012b).
