Leadership changes over time. Names in a mission’s public account may refer to chairpersons, project directors, launch-vehicle directors, payload principal investigators or centre directors; these are different jobs. A responsible historical account should name a person only for a documented role rather than implying that a single leader personally designed an entire mission.

chunks.heading: 3. Institutional development and leadership > 3.3 The role of industry and universities
chunks.text: As the programme expanded, Indian industry became essential for precision components, electronics, structures, materials, test equipment and production. Universities and research laboratories contribute scientific instruments, data analysis and specialist knowledge. The more recent policy environment has encouraged a wider commercial ecosystem while ISRO continues to provide core public capabilities and high-risk research.

chunks.heading: 4. How ISRO is organised
chunks.text:
The Department of Space oversees the national space programme and associated institutions. ISRO’s centres have specialised responsibilities; names and organisational arrangements can change over time, so this section describes the broad functional structure rather than treating every administrative boundary as permanent.
- Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre (VSSC), Thiruvananthapuram: Launch-vehicle design and development.
- U R Rao Satellite Centre (URSC), Bengaluru: Spacecraft design, integration and development.
- Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC SHAR), Sriharikota: Launch complex, vehicle integration, launch operations and range safety.
- Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre (LPSC): Liquid and cryogenic propulsion systems.
- ISRO Propulsion Complex (IPRC), Mahendragiri: Testing and qualification of propulsion systems.
- Space Applications Centre (SAC), Ahmedabad: Payloads and applications, including communications and Earth observation instruments.
- National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC), Hyderabad: Remote-sensing data reception, processing and applications.

chunks.heading: 4. How ISRO is organised
chunks.text:
- National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC), Hyderabad: Remote-sensing data reception, processing and applications.
- ISTRAC, Bengaluru: Telemetry, tracking, command and mission operations support.
- Master Control Facility (MCF): Operations of selected geostationary satellites.
- Human Space Flight Centre (HSFC): Human-spaceflight programme development and coordination.
- Physical Research Laboratory (PRL): Space and planetary science, astronomy and related research.
- National Atmospheric Research Laboratory (NARL): Atmospheric and space-weather-related research.
- NewSpace India Limited (NSIL): Commercial arm for space products and services under the Department of Space.
- IN-SPACe: Promotion, authorisation and facilitation of non-governmental space activity.

chunks.heading: 4. How ISRO is organised > 4.1 From design to launch: a typical mission lifecycle
chunks.text:
- Define the scientific or operational need and translate it into measurable mission objectives.
- Choose orbit, payload, spacecraft architecture, launch vehicle and ground segment.
- Develop requirements, budgets, risk models and verification plans.
- Design and manufacture subsystems; test components and software.
- Integrate the spacecraft and conduct environmental tests such as vibration, acoustic, thermal-vacuum and electromagnetic compatibility testing.
- Integrate the payload and spacecraft with the launch vehicle; perform launch rehearsals and range-safety checks.
- Launch, separate the payload and acquire the spacecraft through ground stations.
- Commission spacecraft systems, deploy instruments or solar arrays as needed, and validate performance.
- Operate the mission, calibrate instruments, distribute data and respond to anomalies.
- End the mission safely: passivate, deorbit, graveyard-orbit or re-enter according to spacecraft type and rules.

chunks.heading: 5. Launch centres, tracking and mission operations > 5.1 Sriharikota
chunks.text: Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC SHAR) at Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh, is India’s principal orbital launch centre. Its coastal location supports launches over the Bay of Bengal and enables launch azimuths suited to a range of orbital inclinations. Launch operations require vehicle assembly buildings, mobile service structures, propellant systems, range instrumentation, weather monitoring, tracking, flight-safety systems and carefully controlled countdown procedures.

chunks.heading: 5. Launch centres, tracking and mission operations > 5.2 Tracking and telemetry
chunks.text: A rocket and spacecraft cannot be operated by watching them visually. Telemetry sends spacecraft and vehicle health data to the ground; tracking measures trajectory and position; command links send instructions. Ground stations and networks support launch, early orbit, manoeuvres, payload operations and recovery. Deep-space missions require long-distance communication, precise antenna pointing, navigation solutions and light-time-aware operations.

chunks.heading: 5. Launch centres, tracking and mission operations > 5.3 Mission control
chunks.text: Mission controllers monitor spacecraft state, power, temperatures, attitude, communications and propulsion. A spacecraft may be healthy but temporarily out of contact because of geometry or planned communication windows. Conversely, a missing signal is an anomaly that must be diagnosed from available telemetry and trajectory information. Mission control uses procedures, simulations, fault trees and carefully reviewed commands to reduce risk.

chunks.heading: 6. Launch vehicles: how India reaches space
chunks.text:
A launch vehicle is a rocket designed to accelerate a payload to the speed and trajectory required for its destination. Rockets work by expelling mass at high speed; they do not push against the air. Staging drops empty tanks and engines to improve performance. The launch vehicle family reflects a progression from small experimental rockets to reliable operational systems and heavier launch capability.
- SLV-3: Role and characteristics: Early four-stage solid-propellant small satellite launcher; Historical significance: Established India’s first indigenous orbital launch capability in 1980.
- ASLV: Role and characteristics: Five-stage technology-development vehicle; Historical significance: Difficult early programme that built knowledge for later launch systems.
- PSLV: Role and characteristics: Versatile multi-stage launcher, with solid and liquid stages; multiple configurations; Historical significance: Reliable workhorse for polar, sun-synchronous and selected transfer-orbit missions; launched Chandrayaan-1 and Mars Orbiter Mission.

chunks.heading: 6. Launch vehicles: how India reaches space
chunks.text:
- PSLV: Role and characteristics: Versatile multi-stage launcher, with solid and liquid stages; multiple configurations; Historical significance: Reliable workhorse for polar, sun-synchronous and selected transfer-orbit missions; launched Chandrayaan-1 and Mars Orbiter Mission.
- GSLV Mk II: Role and characteristics: Launcher using solid, liquid and indigenous cryogenic upper-stage technology; Historical significance: Expanded capability to heavier geostationary-transfer-orbit payloads.
- LVM3 (formerly GSLV Mk III): Role and characteristics: Heavy-lift launcher with two large solid boosters, a liquid core and cryogenic upper stage; Historical significance: Supports heavier communications payloads, commercial launches and the Gaganyaan launcher architecture.
- SSLV: Role and characteristics: Small Satellite Launch Vehicle designed for smaller payloads and quicker, more flexible launch services; Historical significance: Targets the growing small-satellite market and responsive launch demand.

chunks.heading: 6. Launch vehicles: how India reaches space
chunks.text:
- SSLV: Role and characteristics: Small Satellite Launch Vehicle designed for smaller payloads and quicker, more flexible launch services; Historical significance: Targets the growing small-satellite market and responsive launch demand.
- RLV technology demonstrators: Role and characteristics: Experimental reusable launch-vehicle technologies, including landing and autonomous guidance tests; Historical significance: Research towards reducing future launch-system cost; not yet an operational reusable orbital launcher.
- Next-generation launch vehicle concepts: Role and characteristics: Future heavy-lift and semi-cryogenic technologies under development or planning; Historical significance: Aim to expand payload capability and improve economics; timelines and configurations can evolve.

chunks.heading: 6. Launch vehicles: how India reaches space > 6.1 Solid, liquid and cryogenic propulsion
chunks.text: Solid motors store fuel and oxidiser together in a solid grain. They are mechanically robust and provide high thrust, but are difficult to throttle or shut down once ignited. Liquid engines feed fuel and oxidiser from tanks and can often be controlled more flexibly, at the cost of pumps, valves and complex plumbing. Cryogenic engines use propellants at extremely low temperatures, typically liquid oxygen and liquid hydrogen, and provide high efficiency for upper stages. Each technology has different performance, manufacturing, storage and operational challenges.

chunks.heading: 6. Launch vehicles: how India reaches space > 6.2 Payload capacity is orbit-dependent
chunks.text: A rocket’s advertised payload mass is meaningless without the target orbit. Delivering a spacecraft to low Earth orbit is different from placing it into geostationary transfer orbit, a highly elliptical orbit, lunar transfer or an escape trajectory. Inclination, altitude, injection accuracy, fairing size and mission-specific reserves all affect the payload. A spacecraft bound for the Moon needs more energy than a satellite bound for a low Earth orbit.

chunks.heading: 6. Launch vehicles: how India reaches space > 6.3 Why PSLV became important
chunks.text: PSLV developed a reputation for versatility and dependable operations after early developmental setbacks. Its mix of solid and liquid stages supports a range of payloads and mission profiles. It has carried Indian Earth-observation and navigation satellites, scientific missions, lunar and Mars spacecraft, and many international customer satellites. Its record should be understood as a long series of missions, not as a claim that every launch was flawless.

chunks.heading: 6. Launch vehicles: how India reaches space > 6.4 Launch failures and vehicle evolution
chunks.text: Developmental rockets often expose failures in separation systems, control, propulsion, software or staging. The important engineering response is to preserve evidence, reconstruct the flight, identify root causes, implement corrective actions and verify the fix. The 1979 SLV-3 attempt, early ASLV failures and the 1993 PSLV-D1 failure belong to the early learning history; later failures such as the 2010 GSLV-D3, 2010 GSLV-F06, 2021 GSLV-F10, 2022 SSLV-D1 and 2025 PSLV-C61 show that mature programmes still face risk.

chunks.heading: 7. Satellite engineering and orbital mechanics > 7.1 Major spacecraft subsystems
chunks.text:
- Structure: supports the payload and protects components under launch loads.
- Electrical power: solar arrays, batteries, power conditioning and distribution.
- Thermal control: radiators, insulation, heaters and coatings keep equipment within limits.
- Attitude and orbit control: sensors, reaction wheels, thrusters, star trackers, gyros and control software.
- Command and data handling: onboard computers, memory, fault protection and time management.
- Communications: antennas, transponders, radio links and high-rate science-data downlinks.
- Propulsion: thrusters or engines for orbit raising, station keeping, attitude control or deep-space manoeuvres.
- Payload: the instrument or communications system that performs the mission’s main job.

chunks.heading: 7. Satellite engineering and orbital mechanics > 7.2 Common orbits
chunks.text:
- Low Earth orbit (LEO): Typical use: Earth observation, crewed spacecraft, technology demonstrations; Trade-off: Close-up views and lower latency; spacecraft move quickly across the sky and need frequent coverage.
- Sun-synchronous orbit: Typical use: Mapping and imaging at consistent local solar time; Trade-off: Good for comparing imagery over time; requires precise orbital design.
- Geostationary orbit: Typical use: Communications, broadcasting and continuous weather observation over one region; Trade-off: Appears fixed over the equator but requires high energy and is poorly suited to polar coverage.
- Geosynchronous orbit: Typical use: 24-hour orbital period, not necessarily fixed over one point; Trade-off: Can support communications but the ground track may move north-south or east-west.
- Highly elliptical orbit: Typical use: Some communications, science and high-latitude coverage; Trade-off: Long dwell time over one region but more complex coverage and radiation environment.
- Lunar transfer / lunar orbit: Typical use: Moon exploration; Trade-off: Requires navigation, propulsion and careful capture or landing manoeuvres.

chunks.heading: 7. Satellite engineering and orbital mechanics > 7.2 Common orbits
chunks.text:
- Lunar transfer / lunar orbit: Typical use: Moon exploration; Trade-off: Requires navigation, propulsion and careful capture or landing manoeuvres.
- Interplanetary trajectory: Typical use: Mars, solar and other deep-space missions; Trade-off: Long travel times, communication delay and demanding power/thermal design.

chunks.heading: 7. Satellite engineering and orbital mechanics > 7.3 Orbital mechanics in plain language
chunks.text: An orbit is continuous free fall around a body. A satellite stays in orbit because its sideways velocity causes it to keep missing the ground as gravity pulls it inward. Lower orbits generally move faster and have shorter periods; higher circular orbits move more slowly. Changing orbit requires changing velocity, called delta-v. Small manoeuvres can have large effects on long-term trajectory, so navigation and propulsion budgets are central to mission design.

chunks.heading: 7. Satellite engineering and orbital mechanics > 7.4 Why spacecraft separate from rockets
chunks.text: A launcher’s job is to provide the required initial energy and injection conditions. Once a payload separates, the spacecraft must independently generate power, maintain attitude, communicate and perform any necessary manoeuvres. A successful launch does not guarantee mission success; nor does a launch anomaly necessarily mean that every payload is lost. Mission outcome must be assessed from actual spacecraft state and objectives.

chunks.heading: 8. Communications, meteorology and broadcasting
chunks.text: INSAT and GSAT-family satellites support telecommunications, television distribution, data links, meteorology, search-and-rescue-related services and other applications. Satellite communications can connect distant communities and provide resilient links, but services also depend on ground terminals, spectrum coordination, network capacity and operating costs.

chunks.heading: 8. Communications, meteorology and broadcasting > 8.1 INSAT and GSAT
chunks.text: The INSAT system became a cornerstone of India’s communications and meteorological infrastructure. The programme evolved from multipurpose satellites to more specialised communication payloads. GSAT spacecraft support different frequency bands, coverage footprints and user needs. A satellite’s practical usefulness depends on transponder availability, antenna coverage, orbital position, interference control and ground network design.

chunks.heading: 8. Communications, meteorology and broadcasting > 8.2 Weather and disaster warning
chunks.text: Meteorological satellites observe cloud patterns, atmospheric water vapour, sea-surface conditions and other variables. Satellite observations are combined with weather models, ocean data, radar, aircraft and ground stations. The result supports cyclone tracking, rainfall analysis, severe-weather warnings and planning. Satellites are especially valuable over oceans and remote regions where ground observations are sparse.

chunks.heading: 8. Communications, meteorology and broadcasting > 8.3 EDUSAT and social applications
chunks.text: EDUSAT (GSAT-3), launched in 2004, was designed to support education through satellite-enabled connectivity. Space-enabled education, telemedicine and tele-communication projects have demonstrated how satellite systems can help reach remote areas, although their success depends on institutions, local infrastructure, content quality and sustained funding.

chunks.heading: 9. Earth observation and remote sensing
chunks.text: Remote sensing uses instruments aboard satellites to measure reflected sunlight, emitted thermal energy or radar returns. These measurements can reveal land cover, vegetation, soil moisture, water extent, ocean conditions, urban growth, ice and disaster damage. They do not automatically provide ground truth: calibration, atmospheric correction, geolocation, modelling and field measurements are often needed.

chunks.heading: 9. Earth observation and remote sensing > 9.1 Major families
chunks.text:
- IRS — Indian Remote Sensing: Broad family of Earth-observation satellites for resource monitoring and planning.
- Resourcesat: Agriculture, vegetation, land-use and natural-resource assessment.
- Cartosat: High-resolution cartography, mapping, infrastructure and urban planning.
- Oceansat / SCATSAT: Ocean colour, winds, fisheries-related research and ocean-atmosphere studies.
- RISAT / radar imaging: Imaging through cloud cover and at night using synthetic aperture radar.
- EOS-designated missions: Earth-observation spacecraft under ISRO’s evolving naming system.
- INSAT/meteorological imagers and sounders: Weather observation and atmospheric monitoring.

chunks.heading: 9. Earth observation and remote sensing > 9.2 How satellite images become useful information
chunks.text:
- Acquire raw sensor measurements and spacecraft housekeeping data.
- Calibrate sensor values against known standards.
- Correct for spacecraft position, terrain, viewing geometry and atmospheric effects where appropriate.
- Apply algorithms to estimate variables such as vegetation indices, surface temperature or water extent.
- Compare results with field observations, historical baselines and other sensors.
- Deliver maps, time series, alerts or decision-support products to users.

chunks.heading: 9. Earth observation and remote sensing > 9.3 Disaster management
chunks.text: Earth-observation data can support flood mapping, cyclone damage assessment, landslide analysis, wildfire monitoring, drought assessment and post-earthquake planning. Radar can be particularly useful under cloud cover; optical imagery can provide rich visual detail in clear conditions. Neither replaces emergency services, local reports or ground assessment, but rapid and repeatable observations improve situational awareness.

chunks.heading: 9. Earth observation and remote sensing > 9.4 Limits and responsible interpretation
chunks.text: Spatial resolution is not the same as accuracy. A pixel may represent a mixture of land-cover types; a satellite sees only what its sensor and geometry allow; and a single image may be misleading without season, weather and historical context. Responsible use includes uncertainty estimates, privacy safeguards, appropriate data licensing and clear communication about what the imagery can and cannot establish.

chunks.heading: 10. Navigation: IRNSS and NavIC
chunks.text: India’s Regional Navigation Satellite System (IRNSS), now branded NavIC (Navigation with Indian Constellation), was developed to provide positioning, navigation and timing services over India and a surrounding region. It complements rather than simply duplicates global systems such as GPS, Galileo, GLONASS and BeiDou.

chunks.heading: 10. Navigation: IRNSS and NavIC > 10.1 Why an independent regional system?
chunks.text: Navigation signals support transport, surveying, timing, disaster response, maritime activity and location-enabled services. An indigenous regional capability gives India greater control over service design and can add resilience. Actual performance depends on constellation geometry, signal availability, receiver quality, interference, atmospheric conditions and the user environment.

chunks.heading: 10. Navigation: IRNSS and NavIC > 10.2 Constellation and user segment
chunks.text: A navigation system requires satellites, precise orbit and clock determination, ground control, signal design and receivers. Satellites broadcast timing and orbit information; a receiver estimates its position from signal travel times. Several satellites are needed to solve for three-dimensional position and receiver-clock error. NavIC’s regional coverage and service design differ from global constellations.

chunks.heading: 10. Navigation: IRNSS and NavIC > 10.3 NVS-01 and NVS-02
chunks.text: The newer NVS generation is intended to sustain and modernise NavIC services. NVS-01 was launched in 2023. NVS-02 was launched on 29 January 2025; ISRO’s launch register records the launch, but the operational result of a spacecraft should be judged from later official updates rather than the launch entry alone.

chunks.heading: 11. Space science and astronomy > 11.1 AstroSat
chunks.text: AstroSat, launched on 28 September 2015, was India’s dedicated multi-wavelength astronomy observatory. It combined instruments observing different portions of the electromagnetic spectrum, enabling coordinated studies of stars, compact objects, galaxies and high-energy phenomena. Multi-wavelength astronomy matters because different wavelengths reveal different physical processes.

chunks.heading: 11. Space science and astronomy > 11.2 XPoSat
chunks.text: XPoSat was launched on 1 January 2024 to study X-ray polarisation from bright astronomical sources. Polarisation can reveal geometry, magnetic fields and scattering processes around objects such as neutron stars and black holes. Its scientific value lies in measurements that are difficult to obtain with ordinary imaging alone.

chunks.heading: 11. Space science and astronomy > 11.3 X-ray and solar-physics heritage
chunks.text: Aryabhata’s experimental payloads included X-ray astronomy and solar-physics work. Later missions developed a broader scientific capability, with improved detectors, pointing, calibration, data handling and international collaboration. Space astronomy avoids much of the absorption and distortion caused by Earth’s atmosphere, but it requires careful background modelling and instrument calibration.

chunks.heading: 11. Space science and astronomy > 11.4 Scientific data and peer review
chunks.text: A satellite result becomes a scientific contribution through calibration, error analysis, independent checks, data processing, publication and comparison with other observations. Headlines often simplify a finding; technical papers state uncertainty, assumptions and the range of valid interpretation. Mission success can include both instrument performance and the quality of the scientific record it produces.

chunks.heading: 12. Moon exploration: Chandrayaan programme > 12.1 Chandrayaan-1 (2008)
chunks.text: Chandrayaan-1 launched on 22 October 2008 aboard PSLV-C11. It was India’s first lunar exploration mission and carried Indian and international instruments. Its goals included mapping lunar mineralogy and chemistry and investigating the Moon’s surface and environment. Data from instruments including NASA’s Moon Mineralogy Mapper contributed to the discovery of widespread hydroxyl/water-related signatures on the lunar surface. Chandrayaan-1 ended operations earlier than planned, but it achieved important scientific objectives.

chunks.heading: 12. Moon exploration: Chandrayaan programme > 12.2 Chandrayaan-2 (2019)
chunks.text: Chandrayaan-2 launched on 22 July 2019 aboard the GSLV Mk III, now called LVM3. It included an orbiter, Vikram lander and Pragyan rover. The lander’s descent did not end in a successful soft landing, but the orbiter entered lunar orbit and continued to provide scientific observations. This mission is an important example of why a mission must be assessed component by component: one segment can fail while another continues delivering valuable data.

chunks.heading: 12. Moon exploration: Chandrayaan programme > 12.3 Chandrayaan-3 (2023)
chunks.text: Chandrayaan-3 launched on 14 July 2023 aboard LVM3. It consisted of a propulsion module, Vikram lander and Pragyan rover. On 23 August 2023, Vikram achieved a soft landing in the lunar south polar region, making India the fourth country to achieve a soft lunar landing and the first to land successfully in the Moon’s southern high-latitude polar region. Pragyan conducted surface experiments and mobility operations. The mission demonstrated landing capability, hazard-aware descent and surface operations.

chunks.heading: 12. Moon exploration: Chandrayaan programme > 12.4 What the lander and rover measured
chunks.text: The mission’s surface experiments included measurements related to lunar thermal properties, near-surface plasma, seismic activity and elemental composition. Such instruments help scientists understand the physical environment and the Moon’s geological history. The results should be read from instrument papers and ISRO releases; a single surface measurement should not be generalised to the entire Moon.

chunks.heading: 12. Moon exploration: Chandrayaan programme > 12.5 Why the lunar south polar region matters
chunks.text: The lunar poles contain areas that receive little or no direct sunlight and may preserve volatile materials in cold traps. These regions are scientifically valuable but operationally challenging: terrain is rugged, lighting is extreme, temperatures can be harsh and communications can be difficult. A successful landing improves India’s ability to plan more complex lunar missions, but it does not by itself establish the presence of economically recoverable resources.

chunks.heading: 12. Moon exploration: Chandrayaan programme > 12.6 Future Chandrayaan plans
chunks.text: Future Indian lunar work has been discussed in terms of additional exploration, sample-return ambitions and cooperation with other space agencies. Mission architectures, dates and payloads are subject to approval and technical readiness. This reference does not treat a proposed or announced concept as completed until launch and outcome are documented by an official source.

chunks.heading: 13. Mars and planetary exploration > 13.1 Mars Orbiter Mission (Mangalyaan)
chunks.text: India’s Mars Orbiter Mission launched on 5 November 2013 aboard PSLV-C25. After a series of Earth-orbit manoeuvres, it departed for Mars and entered Mars orbit in September 2014. India became the first country to reach Mars orbit on its first attempt. The mission carried instruments to study aspects of the Martian surface and atmosphere, including methane-related measurements, though scientific interpretation of such measurements is complex. Mangalyaan’s significance was not simply a low-cost headline. It demonstrated interplanetary navigation, deep-space communications, spacecraft autonomy, propulsion operations and a disciplined mission architecture. Its operational life exceeded the original planned mission duration, but the spacecraft eventually ceased communicating; official records should be consulted for the exact end-of-mission status and date.

chunks.heading: 13. Mars and planetary exploration > 13.2 Why Mars is difficult
chunks.text: Mars missions must launch within suitable planetary windows, navigate for months, execute trajectory corrections, survive deep-space radiation and temperature cycles, and arrive at the right time and velocity. Orbit insertion or landing requires precise propulsion and navigation. The communications delay prevents joystick-like control from Earth, so spacecraft must execute preplanned sequences autonomously.

chunks.heading: 13. Mars and planetary exploration > 13.3 Venus and other future planetary studies
chunks.text: India has studied future planetary missions, including a proposed Venus mission often referred to as Shukrayaan. Venus is scientifically important because its atmosphere and climate differ dramatically from Earth’s despite broadly similar planetary size. Mission status, funding, launch dates and payloads can change; a proposal is not a launched mission. Future planetary work may depend on instrument readiness, launch capacity, international cooperation and budget decisions.

chunks.heading: 14. Sun and heliophysics: Aditya-L1
chunks.text: Aditya-L1 launched on 2 September 2023 aboard PSLV-XL and was placed into a halo orbit around the Sun–Earth L1 region in January 2024. L1 is a gravitationally useful region approximately 1.5 million kilometres from Earth toward the Sun, where a spacecraft can maintain a favourable view of the Sun with modest station-keeping. It is not a physical point where gravity disappears. The mission studies the solar photosphere, chromosphere and corona, solar wind and magnetic activity using a suite of remote-sensing and in-situ instruments. Understanding solar eruptions and coronal mass ejections improves knowledge of space weather, which can affect satellites, radio communication, navigation systems, astronauts and electrical infrastructure.

chunks.heading: 14. Sun and heliophysics: Aditya-L1 > 14.1 Why the corona is a scientific puzzle
chunks.text: The Sun’s outer atmosphere is much hotter than its visible surface. Magnetic fields, waves, reconnection and plasma processes are among the mechanisms studied to explain this. Solar observations must be coordinated across wavelengths and instruments; one measurement rarely answers the full question.

chunks.heading: 14. Sun and heliophysics: Aditya-L1 > 14.2 Space weather and public infrastructure
chunks.text: Strong solar activity can disturb Earth’s magnetosphere and ionosphere. Potential effects include satellite charging, atmospheric drag changes, radio blackouts, navigation errors and induced currents in power systems. Forecasting depends on observing solar activity and measuring the solar wind between the Sun and Earth. Aditya-L1 contributes to this scientific and operational picture.

chunks.heading: 15. Human spaceflight: Gaganyaan
chunks.text: Gaganyaan is India’s human-spaceflight programme, intended to demonstrate the ability to send Indian astronauts to low Earth orbit and return them safely. Human spaceflight imposes much stricter requirements than an uncrewed satellite: crew escape, life support, pressure integrity, thermal protection, redundant systems, fault tolerance, human factors, recovery and extensive certification are essential.

chunks.heading: 15. Human spaceflight: Gaganyaan > 15.1 Main system elements
chunks.text:
- Human-rated launch vehicle based on LVM3 architecture, with additional safety and reliability provisions.
- Crew module with pressure vessel, avionics, displays, environmental control and life-support interfaces.
- Service module providing power, propulsion and other support during flight.
- Crew escape system capable of moving the crew away from a dangerous launch vehicle.
- Parachute and recovery systems designed for controlled descent and recovery at sea.
- Ground facilities, crew training, mission control, medical support and recovery teams.

chunks.heading: 15. Human spaceflight: Gaganyaan > 15.2 Uncrewed tests before crewed flight
chunks.text: A crewed mission should follow a sequence of progressively more demanding tests. These can include propulsion qualification, pad abort or crew-escape tests, parachute trials, integrated vehicle tests, uncrewed orbital flight, re-entry and recovery validation, and repeated simulations. The order and exact test names may change as engineering evidence accumulates. A planned test is not complete merely because a target date has been announced.

chunks.heading: 15. Human spaceflight: Gaganyaan > 15.3 Crew selection and training
chunks.text: Astronaut candidates must train for spacecraft systems, emergency procedures, physical demands, isolation, microgravity operations, communications and mission-specific tasks. Human-spaceflight safety depends on both hardware and team performance. Crew identities, flight assignments and mission dates should only be treated as final when formally confirmed.

chunks.heading: 15. Human spaceflight: Gaganyaan > 15.4 Long-term ambitions
chunks.text: Gaganyaan is a foundation for potential future human-spaceflight capability, not the same thing as an operational space station. India has discussed longer-term ambitions involving a Bharatiya Antariksh Station and more advanced lunar exploration, but these require substantial new engineering, launch capacity, life-support experience, funding and international or industrial partnerships.

chunks.heading: 16. Docking, re-entry and reusable systems > 16.1 SpaDeX: space docking
chunks.text: The Space Docking Experiment (SpaDeX) launched on 30 December 2024 aboard PSLV-C60, carrying two small spacecraft, commonly identified as SDX-A and SDX-B, with the POEM-4 platform also part of the mission. The objective was to demonstrate technologies for rendezvous, proximity operations and docking. Docking is an enabling capability for future complex missions: assembling large structures, transferring crew or cargo, servicing spacecraft, and conducting sample-return architectures. A docking experiment requires precise relative navigation, inter-spacecraft communications, attitude control, carefully sequenced approach manoeuvres and mechanisms that capture and secure the two vehicles. Demonstration of docking is a technical milestone; it does not automatically mean that every future docking, refuelling or crew-transfer operation is operationally ready.

chunks.heading: 16. Docking, re-entry and reusable systems > 16.2 Re-entry and space capsules
chunks.text: A returning capsule must shed enormous kinetic energy in the atmosphere. Heat shields, shape, thermal materials, guidance, parachutes and recovery operations all contribute to safe return. ISRO’s Space Capsule Recovery Experiment (SRE-1), launched in 2007 and recovered after orbital flight, helped develop re-entry and recovery technologies. The Crew Module Atmospheric Re-entry Experiment (CARE) in 2014 was another key step in the human-spaceflight technology path.

chunks.heading: 16. Docking, re-entry and reusable systems > 16.3 RLV-TD and reusable launch technology
chunks.text: The Reusable Launch Vehicle Technology Demonstrator programme investigates technologies such as autonomous navigation, hypersonic flight, thermal protection and runway landing. The 2016 Hypersonic Flight Experiment and later landing demonstrations contributed to that research. A technology demonstrator is not equivalent to a fully reusable orbital launch system; operational reuse requires repeatable inspection, refurbishment, turnaround, economic validation and reliable performance.

chunks.heading: 16. Docking, re-entry and reusable systems > 16.4 Scramjet and advanced propulsion tests
chunks.text: Scramjet research explores air-breathing propulsion at hypersonic speeds, where atmospheric oxygen can reduce the need to carry oxidiser for part of a flight. Such systems face difficult ignition, combustion, cooling and materials challenges. The experiments are technology steps, not a substitute for conventional orbital launch vehicles today.

chunks.heading: 17. International cooperation and commercial launch services > 17.1 International partnerships
chunks.text: International cooperation has been present since the early sounding-rocket era. Partners can contribute launch services, instruments, tracking support, scientific data, standards and shared mission objectives. Cooperation may be bilateral or multilateral and is governed by technical agreements, export controls, data policies and mission-specific responsibilities.

chunks.heading: 17. International cooperation and commercial launch services > 17.2 NASA–ISRO NISAR
chunks.text: NISAR (NASA–ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar) is a joint Earth-observation mission launched on 30 July 2025 aboard GSLV-F16, according to ISRO’s launch register. It combines radar systems operating at different frequency bands to measure changes in Earth’s land and ice surfaces, vegetation and other dynamic processes. Radar can observe at night and through many cloud conditions. The scientific value comes from repeated, calibrated observations that reveal change over time.

chunks.heading: 17. International cooperation and commercial launch services > 17.3 Proba-3 and precision formation flying
chunks.text: Proba-3 is an ESA mission launched by PSLV-C59 on 5 December 2024. Its objective involves precision formation flying by two spacecraft to create an artificial solar-observation geometry, enabling study of the solar corona. The mission illustrates ISRO’s role as a launch provider for international scientific payloads, while mission ownership and scientific operations remain with the relevant partner agency.

chunks.heading: 17. International cooperation and commercial launch services > 17.4 Commercial launches and customer satellites
chunks.text: ISRO launch vehicles have carried satellites for many countries. Commercial launch services diversify revenue and demonstrate launch reliability, but the primary mission must still meet its technical and contractual requirements. NSIL supports commercialisation of Indian space products and services; ISRO continues research, technology development and public-interest missions.

chunks.heading: 17. International cooperation and commercial launch services > 17.5 New Indian space companies
chunks.text: India’s private space sector includes launch-vehicle developers, satellite manufacturers, earth-data companies, propulsion firms, component suppliers and application startups. The sector can complement public investment by increasing production capacity, attracting capital and testing new business models. Regulatory clarity, access to test facilities, launch cadence, insurance, export markets and predictable procurement remain important factors.

chunks.heading: 18. Mission failures, anomalies and lessons
chunks.text:
Failures are part of space engineering, but their causes and consequences differ. A launch failure may prevent orbit insertion; a spacecraft anomaly may occur after successful separation; a lander may lose control during descent; or a mission may end after completing its primary objectives. Official mission reports and investigation findings should be preferred over speculation.
- Rohini Technology Payload / SLV-3 E1 (1979): Outcome recorded in official launch register: Not accomplished; Lesson / context: Early indigenous orbital-launch development; failure analysis informed later success.
- SLV-3 E2 / Rohini RS-1 (1980): Outcome recorded in official launch register: Successful orbital launch; Lesson / context: Major milestone for indigenous launch capability.
- ASLV-D1 / SROSS-1 (1987): Outcome recorded in official launch register: Not accomplished; Lesson / context: Early, difficult vehicle-development phase.
- ASLV-D2 / SROSS-2 (1988): Outcome recorded in official launch register: Not accomplished; Lesson / context: Further developmental setback; programme continued.

chunks.heading: 18. Mission failures, anomalies and lessons
chunks.text:
- ASLV-D2 / SROSS-2 (1988): Outcome recorded in official launch register: Not accomplished; Lesson / context: Further developmental setback; programme continued.
- PSLV-D1 / IRS-1E (1993): Outcome recorded in official launch register: Not accomplished; Lesson / context: First PSLV development flight did not achieve its intended orbit; later flights matured the system.
- GSLV-F02 / INSAT-4C (2006): Outcome recorded in official launch register: Not accomplished; Lesson / context: Heavy-launch vehicle development remained challenging.
- GSLV-D3 / GSAT-4 (2010): Outcome recorded in official launch register: Not accomplished; Lesson / context: Indigenous cryogenic upper-stage development exposed performance challenges.
- GSLV-F06 / GSAT-5P (2010): Outcome recorded in official launch register: Not accomplished; Lesson / context: Another launch failure led to further vehicle review and corrective work.
- PSLV-C39 / IRNSS-1H (2017): Outcome recorded in official launch register: Not accomplished; Lesson / context: Payload fairing separation issue prevented the satellite from reaching its intended orbit.

chunks.heading: 18. Mission failures, anomalies and lessons
chunks.text:
- PSLV-C39 / IRNSS-1H (2017): Outcome recorded in official launch register: Not accomplished; Lesson / context: Payload fairing separation issue prevented the satellite from reaching its intended orbit.
- Chandrayaan-2 lander (2019): Outcome recorded in official launch register: Orbiter succeeded; lander did not achieve soft landing; Lesson / context: A multi-element mission can have mixed outcomes; the orbiter continued science operations.
- GSLV-F10 / EOS-03 (2021): Outcome recorded in official launch register: Mission unsuccessful; Lesson / context: Cryogenic upper-stage anomaly prevented the intended mission outcome.
- SSLV-D1 / EOS-02 (2022): Outcome recorded in official launch register: Mission unsuccessful; Lesson / context: Early SSLV flight exposed a mission-management/control issue; follow-up flight incorporated changes.
- PSLV-C61 / EOS-09 (2025): Outcome recorded in official launch register: Official register marks not accomplished; Lesson / context: Consult official mission updates for the investigation and detailed cause.

chunks.heading: 18. Mission failures, anomalies and lessons
chunks.text: - PSLV-C61 / EOS-09 (2025): Outcome recorded in official launch register: Official register marks not accomplished; Lesson / context: Consult official mission updates for the investigation and detailed cause.

chunks.heading: 18. Mission failures, anomalies and lessons > 18.1 How a failure investigation works
chunks.text:
- Secure telemetry, tracking, range and ground-system data.
- Reconstruct the sequence of events and identify the earliest unexplained deviation.
- Separate observed facts from hypotheses; compare redundant sensors and independent logs.
- Test candidate failure modes through simulation, hardware examination and engineering analysis.
- Determine root cause and contributing factors, including process or organisational issues where supported.
- Implement corrective actions and verify them through analysis, test and review.
- Communicate the result clearly and update future mission procedures.

chunks.heading: 18. Mission failures, anomalies and lessons > 18.2 Avoiding simplistic success/failure labels
chunks.text: A mission can meet some objectives but not others. Chandrayaan-2’s orbiter continued to deliver data despite the lander loss. A launch vehicle may reach orbit while a payload later experiences a fault. A technology demonstrator may be valuable even when it does not achieve every test objective, provided the experiment produces useful evidence. The most accurate summary states exactly what worked, what did not, and what the mission was intended to demonstrate.

chunks.heading: 19. ISRO’s societal and economic impact > 19.1 Agriculture and natural resources
chunks.text: Remote sensing supports crop-area estimation, vegetation monitoring, drought assessment, soil and water studies, irrigation planning, fisheries advisories and land-use mapping. These are decision-support inputs, not replacements for field surveys or agricultural expertise. Accuracy depends on season, sensor resolution, crop type, processing method and timely ground validation.

chunks.heading: 19. ISRO’s societal and economic impact > 19.2 Disaster risk reduction
chunks.text: Satellite data supports cyclone monitoring, flood extent mapping, landslide assessment, wildfire observation, drought monitoring and damage analysis. Communication satellites can also provide links when terrestrial networks are damaged. Effective response requires data pipelines, trained analysts, pre-agreed responsibilities and clear communication to local authorities.

chunks.heading: 19. ISRO’s societal and economic impact > 19.3 Communications, education and health
chunks.text: Satellite communications can extend television, broadband, tele-education and telemedicine to remote locations. Their value is greatest where terrestrial infrastructure is expensive or unreliable. Yet a link alone is not enough: users need electricity, terminals, technical support, content and sustainable service models.

chunks.heading: 19. ISRO’s societal and economic impact > 19.4 Economic spillovers
chunks.text: Space programmes stimulate high-reliability manufacturing, materials science, electronics, software, precision machining, data analytics and systems engineering. Benefits may include skilled employment, supplier capability and technology transfer. They should be evaluated alongside programme cost, opportunity cost, long-term operations and measurable public outcomes rather than assumed automatically.

chunks.heading: 19. ISRO’s societal and economic impact > 19.5 Environmental and orbital responsibility
chunks.text: Space activity also creates responsibilities: avoid generating debris, passivate spacecraft, coordinate radio spectrum, manage launch emissions and protect sensitive environments. Crowded orbits increase collision risk. Sustainable operations require design choices, tracking, end-of-life planning and international norms.

chunks.heading: 22. Future roadmap and open challenges > 22.1 Human spaceflight and station ambitions
chunks.text: Gaganyaan is the immediate human-spaceflight foundation. A future Indian space station concept would require modular assembly, long-duration life support, orbital logistics, crew health research, cargo transport, power systems and sustained operations. These are substantially more complex than a short crewed mission and should be treated as long-term ambitions until formal milestones are completed.

chunks.heading: 22. Future roadmap and open challenges > 22.2 Lunar sample return and advanced exploration
chunks.text: Sample-return missions require landing, collecting and sealing material, launching from the lunar surface, rendezvous or transfer operations, Earth return and safe recovery. Each step adds risk and complexity. Such plans are valuable long-term goals but depend on technology demonstrations, mission architecture and international coordination.

chunks.heading: 22. Future roadmap and open challenges > 22.3 Launch capacity, reusability and cost
chunks.text: Future competitiveness depends on launch cadence, production scale, reliability, turnaround time, payload integration, range availability and cost. Reusability may lower cost under the right operational model, but development and refurbishment are expensive. A reusable vehicle is economically successful only when its lifecycle cost and flight rate justify the investment.

chunks.heading: 22. Future roadmap and open challenges > 22.4 Private-sector participation
chunks.text: The growth of private launch and satellite companies can broaden innovation and production capacity. The public sector can focus on long-horizon science and high-risk technology while commercial companies address specific markets. A healthy ecosystem needs transparent procurement, access to test facilities, standards, insurance, export pathways, spectrum coordination and sustained demand.

chunks.heading: 22. Future roadmap and open challenges > 22.5 Science priorities
chunks.text:
- Solar and space-weather monitoring to improve understanding of the Sun–Earth system.
- Planetary missions that answer clear scientific questions and build capability incrementally.
- Earth-observation missions with open, calibrated data and operational products for public benefit.
- Navigation resilience and modernised user equipment.
- Space-debris mitigation and sustainable end-of-life disposal.
- Advanced propulsion, autonomous navigation, robotics, docking and precision formation flying.
- Better links between satellite data, universities, public agencies, private innovators and local users.

chunks.heading: 22. Future roadmap and open challenges > 22.6 What remains difficult
chunks.text: The major challenges are not only scientific. They include sustained funding, manufacturing scale, supply-chain resilience, talent development, launch reliability, deep-space communications, human-rating standards, radiation protection, mission autonomy, debris management and converting technical capability into widely used services. Long-term success depends on disciplined testing and learning, not just ambitious announcements.

chunks.heading: 23. Glossary
chunks.text:
- Aditya-L1: India’s solar observatory mission operating around the Sun–Earth L1 region.
- Apogee: The farthest point from Earth in an elliptical Earth orbit.
- Attitude control: Maintaining a spacecraft’s orientation.
- Avionics: Electronic systems used for guidance, navigation, control and monitoring.
- Cryogenic engine: Rocket engine using propellants stored at very low temperatures.
- Delta-v: A measure of velocity change; central to propulsion and mission planning.
- Deep-space network: Ground antennas and systems used to communicate with distant spacecraft.
- EDUSAT: Satellite programme designed for education-related connectivity.
- EOS: Earth Observation Satellite naming designation used in recent ISRO missions.
- Geostationary orbit: Circular equatorial orbit with a 24-hour period, appearing fixed above one longitude.
- GSLV: Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle.
- Halo orbit: A three-dimensional periodic orbit near a libration point in a multi-body gravitational system.
- INSAT: Indian National Satellite system.

chunks.heading: 23. Glossary
chunks.text:
- INSAT: Indian National Satellite system.
- IRNSS / NavIC: Indian Regional Navigation Satellite System / Navigation with Indian Constellation.
- ISRO: Indian Space Research Organisation.
- LEO: Low Earth orbit.
- L1: First Sun–Earth collinear Lagrange region, useful for solar observation.
- LVM3: India’s heavy-lift launch vehicle, formerly called GSLV Mk III.
- Payload: The instrument or spacecraft carried to perform the mission’s main purpose.
- POEM: PSLV Orbital Experimental Module, a platform for experiments in orbit.
- PSLV: Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle.
- Remote sensing: Measuring Earth or other objects from a distance, often with satellite instruments.
- Rendezvous: Bringing two spacecraft into a coordinated nearby trajectory.
- Re-entry: Return through an atmosphere from space.
- SAR: Synthetic aperture radar, a radar imaging technique.
- Satellite bus: The spacecraft platform that supports the mission payload.
- SLV-3: India’s early Satellite Launch Vehicle.
- SSLV: Small Satellite Launch Vehicle.

chunks.heading: 23. Glossary
chunks.text:
- SSLV: Small Satellite Launch Vehicle.
- Sun-synchronous orbit: Orbit arranged so a satellite passes over locations at similar local solar times.
- Telemetry: Data transmitted from a vehicle or spacecraft to the ground.
- Thermal-vacuum test: Test that simulates vacuum and thermal conditions of space.
- Transfer orbit: Intermediate orbit used to move between orbital regimes.
- VSSC: Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre.

chunks.heading: 24. Suggested official sources and research trail > Research and verification note
chunks.text: This is an educational synthesis, not an official ISRO publication. The launch register is a time-sensitive source and may be updated. Some mission pages move as ISRO refreshes its website; if a direct link changes, search the official ISRO domain by mission name. For precise status, consult dated mission updates, annual reports and post-flight statements. Future schedules are inherently provisional.

chunks.heading: Closing perspective
chunks.text: India’s space programme is a story of gradual capability-building: from sounding rockets to satellites, from launch experiments to dependable operational vehicles, from Earth observation to lunar and interplanetary science, and from uncrewed systems toward human spaceflight. Its strongest achievements combine technical ambition with practical applications and institutional learning. The next chapter will be written not only by spectacular missions, but also by reliability, scientific quality, sustainable operations and the ability to make space-derived knowledge useful on Earth.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: ISRO EXPANDED MISSION ENCYCLOPEDIA A detailed companion to Points 20 and 21 of the ISRO Comprehensive Reference Point 20 — Official launch chronology Point 21 — Major spacecraft and programme catalogue Expanded educational edition • 11 October 2026 This volume expands the two catalogue sections of the original ISRO reference into a more explanatory guide. It explains how to read launch records, groups launches by historical era, adds context to each launch entry, and describes the purpose, technology, importance and limitations of major spacecraft programmes. Important limitation: mission catalogues are living records. The chronology below follows the 106-entry launch-register snapshot described in the original document, with the latest listed entry GSLV-F17/EOS-05 dated 4 September 2026. For the most current status, outcomes, spacecraft health and mission-end dates, use ISRO’s official pages and dated mission updates.

chunks.heading: How this companion volume is organised
chunks.text:
- Part A — Reading the launch register: what a launch number means, how to interpret outcomes, and why payloads and launches are not the same thing.
- Part B — Chronology explained by era: early launch vehicles, PSLV maturation, geostationary launchers, science missions, small launchers and recent launches.
- Part C — Launch register entries 1–106: compact explanatory notes for each launch event.
- Part D — Major spacecraft and programmes: detailed thematic entries on satellite families, science missions, planetary exploration, navigation, technology demonstrators and future programmes.
- Part E — Cross-reference tables, terminology and official research sources.

chunks.heading: How this companion volume is organised > A crucial distinction: launch, spacecraft, payload and programme
chunks.text:
A launch is the event in which a rocket attempts to deliver one or more payloads. A spacecraft is a vehicle or satellite that may operate for years. A payload is the instrument, satellite or experiment carried by a launch vehicle. A programme is a family of missions or an enduring capability. These units do not map one-to-one. For example, a single PSLV launch can carry a primary satellite and many co-passengers; the launch register may count it as one launch mission, while satellite catalogues count multiple spacecraft.
- Launch event: What it counts: One rocket launch attempt; Example of why it matters: One launch can carry dozens of satellites.
- Spacecraft: What it counts: An individual satellite, probe, capsule or vehicle; Example of why it matters: Chandrayaan-2 included an orbiter, lander and rover.
- Payload: What it counts: Equipment or spacecraft delivered by a launcher; Example of why it matters: A launch can carry a science instrument platform and customer satellites.
- Programme / family: What it counts: A continuing line of related missions; Example of why it matters: Cartosat and INSAT each span multiple spacecraft.

chunks.heading: How this companion volume is organised > A crucial distinction: launch, spacecraft, payload and programme
chunks.text:
- Programme / family: What it counts: A continuing line of related missions; Example of why it matters: Cartosat and INSAT each span multiple spacecraft.
- Mission objective: What it counts: The specific job the spacecraft is designed to do; Example of why it matters: A satellite can launch successfully but fail to complete its objective.
- Operational service: What it counts: A sustained capability delivered to users; Example of why it matters: Navigation and weather services depend on constellations, ground systems and users.

chunks.heading: How this companion volume is organised > How to interpret outcome labels
chunks.text:
- Successful launch: the launch vehicle delivered its payload(s) to the intended orbit or trajectory, as assessed by the official source.
- Mission unsuccessful / not accomplished: the official register indicates that the intended launch objective was not achieved. The cause should be taken from a formal investigation, not inferred from the label.
- Mixed outcome: one part of a mission may succeed while another fails. Chandrayaan-2 is a prominent example because its orbiter continued science after the lander failed to make a soft landing.
- Launch success does not prove long-term spacecraft health. A satellite can suffer a later power, propulsion, communications or payload anomaly.
- Absence of a failure label in a compact table should not be treated as a full mission-performance assessment.

chunks.heading: PART A — Point 20: Official launch chronology > 1. Why a chronology matters
chunks.text: The chronology shows how India’s space capabilities accumulated. Early missions developed basic launch and spacecraft skills; the PSLV era built dependable access to polar and sun-synchronous orbits; GSLV and LVM3 expanded heavier payload capability; and more recent launches have supported navigation, lunar and solar exploration, commercial services, docking demonstrations and international science missions.

chunks.heading: PART A — Point 20: Official launch chronology > 2. Era-by-era overview
chunks.text:
- 1979–1983: Typical emphasis: First indigenous orbital launcher development; Representative milestones: SLV-3 flight tests and Rohini satellites.
- 1987–1994: Typical emphasis: ASLV experimentation and PSLV beginnings; Representative milestones: SROSS experiments; first PSLV flight and follow-up development.
- 1997–2007: Typical emphasis: Operational satellite launches and launcher maturation; Representative milestones: IRS, INSAT/GSAT, early GSLV, Cartosat, SRE-1.
- 2008–2014: Typical emphasis: Deep-space and navigation expansion; Representative milestones: Chandrayaan-1, Oceansat, IRNSS/NavIC beginnings, Mars Orbiter Mission.
- 2015–2018: Typical emphasis: Science missions, heavier launch capability and constellation launches; Representative milestones: AstroSat, IRNSS completion phase, LVM3 operational development, RLV and scramjet tests.
- 2019–2022: Typical emphasis: Lunar science, Earth observation and small launchers; Representative milestones: Chandrayaan-2, EOS missions, SSLV developmental flights.

chunks.heading: PART A — Point 20: Official launch chronology > 2. Era-by-era overview
chunks.text:
- 2019–2022: Typical emphasis: Lunar science, Earth observation and small launchers; Representative milestones: Chandrayaan-2, EOS missions, SSLV developmental flights.
- 2023–2024: Typical emphasis: Lunar landing, solar science, X-ray astronomy and docking technology; Representative milestones: Chandrayaan-3, Aditya-L1, XPoSat, Proba-3 and SpaDeX.
- 2025–2026 register snapshot: Typical emphasis: Joint radar science, navigation and continued operational launches; Representative milestones: NISAR, CMS-03, BlueBird Block 2, EOS-N1 and EOS-05 in the stated snapshot.

chunks.heading: PART A — Point 20: Official launch chronology > 3. The early indigenous launcher period
chunks.text: The SLV-3 programme established the foundations of orbital launch capability. Early launch attempts provided evidence about staging, guidance, propulsion, separation and ground procedures. Rohini satellites served as technology and scientific payloads in this process. The first attempt in 1979 did not achieve its objective, while the 1980 SLV-3 flight successfully placed Rohini RS-1 in orbit. The broader lesson is that launch capability is built through repeated testing and systematic correction. The ASLV programme was a bridge between the small SLV-3 and the more capable PSLV. Its early failures exposed difficulties in vehicle control, staging and flight dynamics. Although the ASLV itself did not become the main operational launcher, its work contributed to India’s engineering experience and later vehicle development.

chunks.heading: PART A — Point 20: Official launch chronology > 4. The PSLV era
chunks.text: PSLV became central to Indian space access because it could place a variety of payloads into polar and sun-synchronous orbits and could be adapted to different mission profiles. It launched Earth-observation satellites, navigation satellites, Chandrayaan-1, the Mars Orbiter Mission, AstroSat, Aditya-L1, XPoSat, Proba-3 and SpaDeX. Its record also includes developmental failure and later anomalies, so its reputation is best understood as the result of long-term maturation and a large operational record. PSLV’s mixed solid/liquid staging allows engineers to balance high thrust at liftoff with controlled burns and efficient upper-stage operation. Mission-specific configuration, payload mass, target orbit and co-passenger deployment sequence determine how a particular flight is arranged.

chunks.heading: PART A — Point 20: Official launch chronology > 5. GSLV and LVM3: heavier payloads
chunks.text: GSLV Mk II was developed to carry heavier payloads into geosynchronous transfer orbit and relies on an indigenous cryogenic upper stage. Cryogenic propulsion is technically demanding because propellants must be stored at very low temperatures and fed through tightly controlled engine systems. Early GSLV failures were costly, but later missions demonstrated a more mature capability. LVM3, previously called GSLV Mk III, is a heavier launcher with two solid strap-on boosters, a liquid core and a cryogenic upper stage. It launched Chandrayaan-2 and Chandrayaan-3, supported OneWeb satellite deployments and later commercial payloads. It is also the basis for the launch-vehicle architecture intended for Gaganyaan, with human-rating changes and additional safety qualification required.

chunks.heading: PART A — Point 20: Official launch chronology > 6. Science and exploration launch events
chunks.text: The chronology marks a shift from technology development and operational satellite services toward dedicated scientific exploration. Chandrayaan-1 began India’s lunar exploration programme; the Mars Orbiter Mission demonstrated interplanetary operations; AstroSat and XPoSat support astronomy; Aditya-L1 studies the Sun; and Chandrayaan-3 demonstrated a lunar soft landing. These missions require more than launch performance: they depend on long-duration power, thermal management, autonomy, communications, navigation and specialised scientific instruments.

chunks.heading: PART A — Point 20: Official launch chronology > 7. Technology demonstrations
chunks.text: Some entries are not ordinary satellite launches. RLV-TD tests reusable-launch technologies; scramjet experiments study air-breathing propulsion at hypersonic speed; CARE and SRE-1 developed re-entry and recovery capability; the Crew Escape System test addressed astronaut safety; POEM provides an orbital platform for experiments; and SpaDeX tested rendezvous and docking. A technology demonstration can be successful even when it is not an operational service, but its claims must remain limited to what was actually tested.

chunks.heading: PART A — Point 20: Official launch chronology > 8. Recent entries and verification
chunks.text: The 2025–2026 entries in the snapshot include EOS-09, NISAR, CMS-03, BlueBird Block 2, EOS-N1 and EOS-05. The existence of a launch-register entry establishes that the event is recorded, but readers should consult the latest mission update for orbit, commissioning, anomalies and operational status. In particular, launch outcomes and payload status can be revised after the first public summary.
