chunks.heading: PART C — Point 21: Major spacecraft and programme catalogue
chunks.text: This part expands the short programme index into explanations of purpose, instruments or technical approach, historical importance, applications, limitations and links to related missions. A satellite family can include many spacecraft with different instruments and operational lives; the summaries below describe the programme-level role rather than every configuration detail.

chunks.heading: PART C — Point 21: Major spacecraft and programme catalogue > 1. Aryabhata
chunks.text: Period / status: 1975 • Category: Experimental science satellite Overview: India’s first satellite, designed and built in India and launched from the Soviet Union on 19 April 1975. It carried experiments associated with X-ray astronomy, aeronomy and solar physics. Why it matters: It developed spacecraft design, integration, telemetry, power and command experience. It was not an operational communications satellite. Its importance is institutional and technical: India demonstrated that it could design a satellite and operate a space mission with international launch support. Applications / legacy: Spacecraft engineering heritage; early space-science capability.

chunks.heading: PART C — Point 21: Major spacecraft and programme catalogue > 2. Bhaskara-I and Bhaskara-II
chunks.text: Period / status: 1979 and 1981 • Category: Experimental remote sensing Overview: The Bhaskara satellites carried Earth-observation instruments including television cameras and microwave radiometry-related experiments. They supported early work on land, water and ocean observations. Why it matters: They helped establish the practical value of remote sensing for a country with large agricultural, hydrological and coastal systems. Early instruments and data processing were more limited than modern imaging systems, but the missions provided experience for the later IRS programme. Applications / legacy: Earth observation, resource monitoring, satellite data processing.

chunks.heading: PART C — Point 21: Major spacecraft and programme catalogue > 3. Rohini series
chunks.text: Period / status: 1979 onward • Category: Technology and scientific satellites Overview: Rohini satellites were closely tied to India’s early launch-vehicle development, particularly SLV-3. Some carried technology or scientific payloads used to measure performance and demonstrate basic spacecraft functions. Why it matters: Rohini RS-1’s successful 1980 orbit insertion by SLV-3 is a foundational milestone. The series should be read in the context of launch development, not as a single homogeneous operational satellite fleet. Applications / legacy: Launch-vehicle qualification and indigenous satellite know-how.

chunks.heading: PART C — Point 21: Major spacecraft and programme catalogue > 4. APPLE
chunks.text: Period / status: 1981 • Category: Experimental communications satellite Overview: Ariane Passenger Payload Experiment (APPLE) was India’s experimental geostationary communications satellite. It helped develop three-axis stabilisation, communications payload operations and geostationary satellite practices. Why it matters: APPLE was an important bridge toward multipurpose operational communications satellites. Communications spacecraft must maintain precise pointing, manage transponders, generate power and remain in the assigned orbital slot. Applications / legacy: Communications engineering, satellite broadcasting and domestic expertise.

chunks.heading: PART C — Point 21: Major spacecraft and programme catalogue > 5. INSAT system
chunks.text: Period / status: 1980s onward • Category: Multipurpose operational satellite system Overview: INSAT combined communications, television distribution, meteorology and other services. Over time, different spacecraft and payload configurations served different operational needs. Why it matters: The programme helped make space services part of everyday infrastructure. Its value lies in sustained service availability and the integration of satellite capacity with ground networks, broadcasters, meteorological agencies and public users. Applications / legacy: Telecommunications, broadcasting, weather observation and emergency support.

chunks.heading: PART C — Point 21: Major spacecraft and programme catalogue > 6. GSAT family
chunks.text: Period / status: 2000s onward • Category: Communications and specialised satellites Overview: GSAT spacecraft support a range of communications services, including fixed satellite service, mobile or specialised communications, data relay and other mission-specific payloads. Why it matters: The family reflects growing domestic capability in satellite payloads and heavier spacecraft. Each satellite’s service depends on frequency band, coverage footprint, antenna design, transponder capacity, orbital location and user terminals. Applications / legacy: Communications, data connectivity and specialised networks.

chunks.heading: PART C — Point 21: Major spacecraft and programme catalogue > 7. IRS programme
chunks.text: Period / status: 1988 onward • Category: Indian Remote Sensing Overview: IRS is a broad Earth-observation programme, not one satellite. It evolved from experimental missions to operational systems supporting land, water, agriculture, forests, coastal regions and environmental monitoring. Why it matters: Remote sensing provides repeatable measurements over large areas. Data must be calibrated and interpreted using models and ground validation. A satellite image is not itself a complete decision; it is one input into planning and monitoring. Applications / legacy: Resource mapping, environmental analysis and public planning.

chunks.heading: PART C — Point 21: Major spacecraft and programme catalogue > 8. Resourcesat
chunks.text: Period / status: 2003 onward • Category: Natural resources and agriculture Overview: Resourcesat spacecraft use multispectral imaging to observe vegetation, crop patterns, land use and natural resources. Different sensors provide different spatial and spectral resolutions. Why it matters: Time-series observations can reveal changes in vegetation and crop conditions. Reliable interpretation requires knowledge of crop calendars, weather, field observations and sensor limitations. Applications / legacy: Agriculture, forestry, land cover and water-resource assessment.

chunks.heading: PART C — Point 21: Major spacecraft and programme catalogue > 9. Cartosat
chunks.text: Period / status: 2005 onward • Category: Cartography and high-resolution imaging Overview: Cartosat missions focus on mapping and detailed Earth observation. Some spacecraft provide stereo imagery or high-resolution imaging useful for deriving terrain and mapping features. Why it matters: Applications include urban planning, infrastructure, mapping and change detection. Higher spatial resolution does not automatically mean perfect accuracy; viewing angle, terrain, geolocation and image-processing methods matter. Applications / legacy: Mapping, infrastructure planning and geospatial information.

chunks.heading: PART C — Point 21: Major spacecraft and programme catalogue > 10. Oceansat and SCATSAT
chunks.text: Period / status: 1999 onward • Category: Ocean and atmosphere observation Overview: Oceansat spacecraft have supported ocean-colour and oceanographic observations. SCATSAT-1 focused on ocean-surface wind vector measurements using scatterometer technology. Why it matters: Ocean data contributes to fisheries advisories, marine weather, climate research and ocean-state assessment. Measurements are combined with buoys, ships, models and other satellites. Applications / legacy: Ocean science, fisheries-related services, weather and climate.

chunks.heading: PART C — Point 21: Major spacecraft and programme catalogue > 11. RISAT and radar imaging
chunks.text: Period / status: 2009 onward • Category: Synthetic aperture radar Overview: RISAT spacecraft use radar imaging. Unlike optical cameras, radar systems transmit or receive microwave signals and can observe in darkness and through many cloud conditions. Why it matters: Radar images are not photographs in the ordinary sense. Interpretation depends on surface roughness, moisture, geometry and radar wavelength. Radar is especially valuable for certain all-weather monitoring tasks but requires specialised processing. Applications / legacy: Flood mapping, agriculture, disaster response and all-weather imaging.

chunks.heading: PART C — Point 21: Major spacecraft and programme catalogue > 12. NavIC / IRNSS
chunks.text: Period / status: 2013 onward • Category: Regional navigation and timing Overview: NavIC is India’s regional satellite-navigation system. It combines a satellite constellation, ground control, timing and navigation signals, and compatible receivers. Why it matters: Navigation satellites broadcast precisely timed signals and orbit information; receivers estimate position from signal travel time. System performance depends on constellation geometry, clock accuracy, signal quality, interference and receiver capability. Applications / legacy: Positioning, navigation, timing and strategic resilience.

chunks.heading: PART C — Point 21: Major spacecraft and programme catalogue > 13. EDUSAT / GSAT-3
chunks.text: Period / status: 2004 • Category: Education connectivity Overview: EDUSAT was designed for education-related satellite connectivity, including interactive and broadcast educational services. Why it matters: It demonstrated how satellite communications can help connect remote classrooms and institutions. Long-term impact depends on receiving equipment, electricity, curriculum, teacher training and operational support. Applications / legacy: Distance education and public-service communications.

chunks.heading: PART C — Point 21: Major spacecraft and programme catalogue > 14. Kalpana-1 and meteorological satellites
chunks.text: Period / status: 2002 onward • Category: Weather observation Overview: Kalpana-1 and later meteorological payloads supported cloud imaging and weather monitoring. More recent INSAT meteorological spacecraft provide enhanced imaging and sounding capability. Why it matters: Satellites are especially useful over oceans and areas with sparse ground stations. Weather forecasts still depend on numerical models, radar, surface observations and expert interpretation. Applications / legacy: Cyclone monitoring, cloud tracking and weather forecasting.

chunks.heading: PART C — Point 21: Major spacecraft and programme catalogue > 15. Chandrayaan-1
chunks.text: Period / status: 2008 • Category: Lunar orbiter Overview: India’s first lunar exploration mission carried Indian and international instruments to map the Moon’s mineralogy and surface environment. It launched on 22 October 2008. Why it matters: Data from instruments including the Moon Mineralogy Mapper contributed to evidence of water-related signatures on the lunar surface. The mission ended earlier than planned but delivered important science. Applications / legacy: Lunar mineralogy, water-related science and deep-space operations.

chunks.heading: PART C — Point 21: Major spacecraft and programme catalogue > 16. Mars Orbiter Mission / Mangalyaan
chunks.text: Period / status: 2013 • Category: Mars orbiter Overview: Launched on 5 November 2013, the Mars Orbiter Mission used a series of Earth-orbit manoeuvres before trans-Mars injection and Mars orbit insertion in September 2014. Why it matters: It demonstrated interplanetary navigation, autonomous spacecraft operations, deep-space communications and trajectory design. India reached Mars orbit on its first attempt. The spacecraft’s scientific findings should be assessed instrument by instrument. Applications / legacy: Planetary science and deep-space mission capability.

chunks.heading: PART C — Point 21: Major spacecraft and programme catalogue > 17. AstroSat
chunks.text: Period / status: 2015 • Category: Multi-wavelength astronomy Overview: AstroSat is India’s dedicated multi-wavelength space observatory, with instruments observing different energy bands and enabling coordinated studies of astronomical objects. Why it matters: Different wavelengths reveal different physical processes. Combining observations improves understanding of compact objects, stars and galaxies, but results depend on calibration, background modelling and peer-reviewed analysis. Applications / legacy: Astronomy and high-energy astrophysics.

chunks.heading: PART C — Point 21: Major spacecraft and programme catalogue > 18. Chandrayaan-2
chunks.text: Period / status: 2019 • Category: Lunar orbiter, lander and rover Overview: Chandrayaan-2 included an orbiter, Vikram lander and Pragyan rover. The spacecraft launched on 22 July 2019. The lander did not complete a soft landing, but the orbiter entered lunar orbit and continued science operations. Why it matters: The mission illustrates the importance of separating component outcomes. The orbiter’s observations remained scientifically valuable, while the landing attempt supplied lessons for later descent engineering. Applications / legacy: Lunar remote sensing, surface-science preparation and landing-system learning.

chunks.heading: PART C — Point 21: Major spacecraft and programme catalogue > 19. Chandrayaan-3
chunks.text: Period / status: 2023 • Category: Lunar landing and surface science Overview: Chandrayaan-3 launched on 14 July 2023 and achieved a soft landing on 23 August 2023. The mission comprised a propulsion module, Vikram lander and Pragyan rover. Why it matters: It demonstrated India’s ability to conduct a lunar soft landing and surface operations in the Moon’s southern high-latitude region. The lander and rover conducted in-situ measurements of thermal, seismic, plasma and elemental properties. Applications / legacy: Landing technology, lunar surface science and future exploration capability.

chunks.heading: PART C — Point 21: Major spacecraft and programme catalogue > 20. Aditya-L1
chunks.text: Period / status: 2023 onward • Category: Solar observatory Overview: Aditya-L1 launched on 2 September 2023 and entered a halo orbit around the Sun–Earth L1 region in January 2024. It carries remote-sensing and in-situ instruments to study solar layers, solar wind and magnetic activity. Why it matters: Solar eruptions can affect satellites, radio communications, navigation and power infrastructure. The mission contributes observations needed to understand solar physics and improve space-weather knowledge. Applications / legacy: Heliophysics and Sun–Earth environment studies.

chunks.heading: PART C — Point 21: Major spacecraft and programme catalogue > 21. XPoSat
chunks.text: Period / status: 2024 onward • Category: X-ray polarimetry Overview: XPoSat launched on 1 January 2024 to measure X-ray polarisation from bright cosmic sources. Polarisation can reveal source geometry, magnetic fields and scattering processes. Why it matters: The mission adds a measurement type that complements imaging, timing and spectroscopy. Science results require calibration and careful separation of source signals from background noise. Applications / legacy: High-energy astrophysics and compact-object studies.

chunks.heading: PART C — Point 21: Major spacecraft and programme catalogue > 22. INSAT-3DS
chunks.text: Period / status: 2024 onward • Category: Meteorological satellite Overview: INSAT-3DS is a meteorological mission designed to support weather observation, atmospheric monitoring and related operational services. Why it matters: Its value depends on the continuity of observations and their integration with forecasting systems. Satellite imagery is combined with ground weather stations, radar, ocean observations and numerical models. Applications / legacy: Weather forecasting and disaster preparedness.

chunks.heading: PART C — Point 21: Major spacecraft and programme catalogue > 23. SpaDeX
chunks.text: Period / status: 2024 onward • Category: Rendezvous and docking technology Overview: SpaDeX launched on 30 December 2024 with two spacecraft intended to demonstrate rendezvous, proximity operations and docking. Why it matters: Docking requires relative navigation, attitude control, communication, precise manoeuvres and capture mechanisms. It is an enabling technology for assembling structures, servicing spacecraft and complex sample-return or station missions. Applications / legacy: Autonomous rendezvous, docking and future mission architecture.

chunks.heading: PART C — Point 21: Major spacecraft and programme catalogue > 24. Proba-3
chunks.text: Period / status: 2024 onward • Category: Precision formation flying Overview: ESA’s Proba-3 mission launched from India aboard PSLV-C59 on 5 December 2024. Two spacecraft fly in precise formation to create a solar-coronagraph geometry. Why it matters: This is an example of an international customer mission using an Indian launch service. Formation flying requires accurate relative positioning and coordinated operations; scientific ownership and operations belong to the partner mission team. Applications / legacy: Solar-corona research and commercial launch cooperation.

chunks.heading: PART C — Point 21: Major spacecraft and programme catalogue > 25. NISAR
chunks.text: Period / status: 2025 onward • Category: Joint NASA–ISRO radar Earth science Overview: NISAR launched on 30 July 2025 aboard GSLV-F16 in the chronology snapshot. It combines radar systems at different frequency bands to observe changes in Earth’s land and ice surfaces, vegetation and other dynamic systems. Why it matters: Repeated radar measurements can reveal subtle changes in surface displacement and ecosystem structure. Its value comes from consistent global observations, calibration, open scientific use and integration with other Earth data. Applications / legacy: Earth-system science, land deformation, ice and ecosystem monitoring.

chunks.heading: PART C — Point 21: Major spacecraft and programme catalogue > 26. SRE-1 and CARE
chunks.text: Period / status: 2007 and 2014 • Category: Re-entry and recovery experiments Overview: SRE-1 demonstrated orbital capsule recovery, while CARE tested a crew-module-shaped body’s atmospheric re-entry behaviour. Both supported knowledge relevant to returning payloads from space. Why it matters: Re-entry demands thermal protection, guidance, deceleration and recovery. These experiments were technology steps and do not alone establish a complete crewed spacecraft system. Applications / legacy: Capsule design, heat shields, parachutes and recovery operations.

chunks.heading: PART C — Point 21: Major spacecraft and programme catalogue > 27. RLV-TD
chunks.text: Period / status: 2016 onward • Category: Reusable launch vehicle technology Overview: RLV-TD experiments investigate hypersonic flight, autonomous guidance, thermal protection and landing technologies. Why it matters: A demonstrator test is not the same as an operational reusable orbital launcher. Reusability must be demonstrated through repeated flights, inspection, refurbishment, reliable turnaround and economic performance. Applications / legacy: Future launch-system research and potential cost reduction.

chunks.heading: PART C — Point 21: Major spacecraft and programme catalogue > 28. Scramjet technology demonstrators
chunks.text: Period / status: 2016 onward • Category: Air-breathing propulsion Overview: Scramjet experiments study supersonic-combustion ramjet operation at hypersonic speeds, where atmospheric oxygen can be used during part of flight. Why it matters: The research faces difficult ignition, mixing, combustion, cooling and material challenges. It complements rather than replaces conventional rocket propulsion for orbital launch today. Applications / legacy: Advanced propulsion research.

chunks.heading: PART C — Point 21: Major spacecraft and programme catalogue > 29. SSLV
chunks.text: Period / status: 2022 onward • Category: Small Satellite Launch Vehicle Overview: SSLV is designed to provide more flexible launch services for small satellites, with an emphasis on simpler integration and shorter preparation cycles. Why it matters: The early developmental flight in 2022 was unsuccessful; the follow-up and later developmental flights tested corrective changes. Operational reliability and market competitiveness depend on repeated performance and launch cadence. Applications / legacy: Small-satellite access and responsive launch services.

chunks.heading: PART C — Point 21: Major spacecraft and programme catalogue > 30. Gaganyaan
chunks.text: Period / status: In development • Category: Human spaceflight Overview: Gaganyaan is intended to demonstrate India’s ability to send astronauts to low Earth orbit and return them safely. It requires a human-rated launch system, crew module, service module, escape system, life support, re-entry, recovery and trained crews. Why it matters: Human spaceflight has much stricter safety requirements than an uncrewed satellite. Uncrewed tests, escape-system trials and integrated qualification are essential. Dates and crew assignments should be treated as provisional until officially confirmed. Applications / legacy: Human spaceflight capability and future orbital missions.

chunks.heading: PART C — Point 21: Major spacecraft and programme catalogue > 31. Future lunar sample-return concepts
chunks.text: Period / status: Proposed / under study • Category: Advanced lunar exploration Overview: Sample-return architecture may require landing, collecting and sealing material, launching from the lunar surface, rendezvous or transfer operations, Earth return and safe recovery. Why it matters: Each stage introduces complexity and risk. A proposal or technology study is not a completed mission, and mission configuration depends on approval, funding, readiness and cooperation. Applications / legacy: Lunar science and advanced autonomous operations.

chunks.heading: PART C — Point 21: Major spacecraft and programme catalogue > 32. Future Venus mission concepts
chunks.text: Period / status: Proposed / under study • Category: Planetary atmosphere and surface research Overview: A Venus mission would investigate the atmosphere, climate and planetary evolution of a world with extreme surface pressure and temperature. The programme has been discussed under names including Shukrayaan. Why it matters: Mission timing, payload and approval can change. Scientific value depends on instruments able to survive the environment and return calibrated data. The proposal should not be described as launched until official records confirm it. Applications / legacy: Comparative planetology and atmospheric science.

chunks.heading: PART D — Cross-reference and comparison > Which programmes serve which broad needs?
chunks.text:
- Where are we, and what time is it? : Relevant programmes: NavIC / IRNSS; What they contribute: Positioning, navigation and timing signals.
- How is land and vegetation changing? : Relevant programmes: IRS, Resourcesat, Cartosat, RISAT, NISAR; What they contribute: Optical, radar and repeated Earth observations.
- What is happening over the ocean? : Relevant programmes: Oceansat, SCATSAT, meteorological satellites; What they contribute: Ocean colour, winds and atmospheric/ocean conditions.
- How can we communicate across large distances? : Relevant programmes: INSAT, GSAT; What they contribute: Satellite communications and broadcasting.
- What is the Moon like? : Relevant programmes: Chandrayaan-1, -2 and -3; What they contribute: Orbital mapping, mineralogy, landing and in-situ surface measurements.
- How does Mars behave? : Relevant programmes: Mars Orbiter Mission; What they contribute: Orbital observation and interplanetary operations.
- How does the Sun affect Earth? : Relevant programmes: Aditya-L1; What they contribute: Solar activity, solar wind and space-weather research.

chunks.heading: PART D — Cross-reference and comparison > Which programmes serve which broad needs?
chunks.text:

- What are extreme cosmic objects doing? : Relevant programmes: AstroSat, XPoSat; What they contribute: Multi-wavelength astronomy and X-ray polarimetry.
- Can spacecraft meet and connect in orbit? : Relevant programmes: SpaDeX; What they contribute: Rendezvous and docking technology.
- Can India return people from orbit? : Relevant programmes: Gaganyaan, CARE, SRE-1, Crew Escape System tests; What they contribute: Crew systems, re-entry, abort and recovery technologies.
- Can launch costs be reduced through reuse? : Relevant programmes: RLV-TD, scramjet research and future launch systems; What they contribute: Technology demonstrations toward future architectures.

chunks.heading: PART D — Cross-reference and comparison > Launch vehicle quick comparison
chunks.text:
- SLV-3: Best understood as: Early indigenous orbital launcher; Common role in the programme: Technology foundation; Important caveat: Historical system, not current operational launcher.
- ASLV: Best understood as: Intermediate developmental vehicle; Common role in the programme: Bridge to later systems; Important caveat: Its difficult record still generated useful engineering experience.
- PSLV: Best understood as: Versatile operational workhorse; Common role in the programme: Earth observation, science, navigation and many commercial payloads; Important caveat: Payload capability depends on orbit and configuration.
- GSLV Mk II: Best understood as: Medium/heavier geosynchronous launcher; Common role in the programme: Communications, meteorology, navigation and selected science missions; Important caveat: Cryogenic upper-stage performance is technically demanding.
- LVM3: Best understood as: Heavy-lift launcher; Common role in the programme: Large spacecraft, commercial constellation deployments and Gaganyaan architecture; Important caveat: Human-rated use requires additional qualification and safety measures.

chunks.heading: PART D — Cross-reference and comparison > Launch vehicle quick comparison
chunks.text:

- SSLV: Best understood as: Small-satellite launcher; Common role in the programme: Small payloads and more responsive launch services; Important caveat: Market and operational performance depend on reliability and launch cadence.

chunks.heading: PART E — Research and source verification > How to research a mission properly
chunks.text:
- Start with the official ISRO launch page to confirm the launch date, vehicle and primary payload.
- Open the dedicated mission page for objectives, instruments and spacecraft architecture.
- Look for dated post-launch updates to confirm injection orbit, commissioning and anomalies.
- Use annual reports for programme-level context and milestone summaries.
- For scientific discoveries, find the instrument paper or peer-reviewed publication and check its stated uncertainty.
- For international missions, read both the launch provider’s account and the mission owner’s account.
- Record the access date, because current spacecraft status and programme schedules change.

chunks.heading: PART E — Research and source verification > Short glossary for catalogue readers
chunks.text:
- Co-passenger: A secondary satellite or payload carried alongside the primary payload.
- Commissioning: Initial checks and calibration after launch before regular service.
- Cryogenic upper stage: A rocket stage using very cold propellants, commonly liquid oxygen and liquid hydrogen.
- Earth observation: Satellite measurement of Earth’s surface, oceans or atmosphere.
- Geostationary transfer orbit: An intermediate orbit used to reach geostationary orbit.
- L1: A Sun–Earth gravitational region useful for solar observation; not a physical platform.
- Payload fairing: Protective shell around the payload during atmospheric ascent.
- POEM: PSLV Orbital Experimental Module, a platform for in-orbit experiments.
- Remote sensing: Obtaining information about a target without direct physical contact.
- Rendezvous: Coordinated approach of two spacecraft to nearby trajectories.
- SAR: Synthetic aperture radar, a radar imaging technique.
- Soft landing: Controlled landing at low enough speed to preserve the lander and its equipment.

chunks.heading: PART E — Research and source verification > Short glossary for catalogue readers
chunks.text:
- Soft landing: Controlled landing at low enough speed to preserve the lander and its equipment.
- Sun-synchronous orbit: An orbit arranged for consistent local solar-time observations.
- Telemetry: Vehicle or spacecraft status data sent to ground controllers.

chunks.heading: Final perspective
chunks.text: The launch chronology is the timeline of how India reached space; the spacecraft catalogue explains what India did with that access. Read together, they show the connection between launch engineering, operational satellite services, scientific instruments, deep-space navigation and the technologies needed for more complex future missions. The most reliable way to judge any mission is to distinguish what was planned, what was launched, what worked, what data were returned and what remains a future objective. This document is an educational synthesis, not an official ISRO publication. The 106-entry register and future-programme status reflect the source snapshot used for the companion volume. Verify all time-sensitive claims, particularly recent launch outcomes, spacecraft health, crew assignments and planned dates, against current official releases.

Replaces INSAT-4A; used for VSAT, TV uplink, DTH, DSNG and telecom. | GSAT-31: Launched 6 Feb 2019 on Ariane-5; about 2,535 kg at 48 E with 40 Ku-band transponders over India and its islands. Used for VSAT, DTH, cellular backhaul, ATMs, stock-exchange networks and e-governance. | GSAT-9 (South Asia Satellite): Launched 5 May 2017 on GSLV-F09; about 2,230 kg at 48 E with 12 Ku transponders. Provides communication, tele-medicine, disaster support and e-learning to neighbouring countries (not Pakistan). | CMS-01 (GSAT-12R): Launched 17 Dec 2020 on PSLV-C50; about 1,410 kg. Extended C-band services over the Indian mainland, Andaman and Nicobar and Lakshadweep islands; replaces GSAT-12. | GSAT-7 (Rukmini): Launched 30 Aug 2013 on Ariane-5; about 2,650 kg at 74 E. UHF, S, C and Ku payloads giving the Indian Navy secure communications over a footprint of about 2,000 nautical miles across the Indian Ocean Region.

chunks.heading: Recommendation case 29: Communications / Regional / GEO / Continuous
chunks.text: UHF, S, C and Ku payloads giving the Indian Navy secure communications over a footprint of about 2,000 nautical miles across the Indian Ocean Region. | CMS-03 (GSAT-7R): Launched 2 Nov 2025 on LVM3-M5; about 4,410 kg, the heaviest satellite launched from Indian soil. Multi-band payloads giving the Navy secure communications across a wide Indian Ocean footprint. ISRO reports that corrective measures drawn from the NVS-02 anomaly were tested on this satellite. | Together: Ku and C-band satellites carry TV, VSAT and telecom traffic; Ka-band high-throughput satellites (GSAT-11, GSAT-29, GSAT-N2) add broadband capacity; naval and air-force satellites add secure links. Overlapping slots between 48 E and 93.5 E give redundancy, load sharing and backup if one satellite is lost. Global scope is Partial because this covers only the Indian Ocean sector.

chunks.heading: Recommendation case 81: Earth Observation (Optical) / Global / LEO / Continuous
chunks.text:
- Application: Earth Observation (Optical)
- Coverage: Global
- Requested orbit: LEO
- Requested revisit: Continuous
- Resolved orbit: LEO
- Feasibility: P (partial)
- Recommended ISRO satellites: Cartosat-3 (~0.28 m PAN), Cartosat-2D/2E/2F (~0.65 m), Resourcesat-2A (LISS-4 5.8 m, LISS-3 23.5 m, AWiFS 56 m), HySIS (hyperspectral), Oceansat-3 (ocean colour)
- Best achievable revisit (hours): 120.0
- Revisit fit: Does not meet
- Rationale: Same limits as SSO Global; EOS-08 is inclined (~37 deg) and cannot reach high latitudes.
- Alternative if unavailable:
- Combination members: Cartosat-3 + Cartosat-2 series (2D, 2E, 2F, 2A) + Resourcesat-2 / 2A + HySIS + Oceansat-3 (EOS-06)
- Combination details: Cartosat-3: Third-generation Cartosat launched 27 Nov 2019 on PSLV-C47 into a sun-synchronous orbit at about 509 km. Panchromatic imaging at about 0.25 to 0.28 m (ISRO's finest) plus multispectral bands, over a swath of roughly 16 km, with agile pointing for off-nadir, stereo and rapid re-targeting.

chunks.heading: Recommendation case 81: Earth Observation (Optical) / Global / LEO / Continuous
chunks.text: Panchromatic imaging at about 0.25 to 0.28 m (ISRO's finest) plus multispectral bands, over a swath of roughly 16 km, with agile pointing for off-nadir, stereo and rapid re-targeting. Best for city-scale mapping, infrastructure, change detection and defence. Limits: narrow swath, daylight and clear sky only, tasked rather than systematic. | Cartosat-2 series (2D, 2E, 2F, 2A): Cartosat-2D (Feb 2017), 2E (Jun 2017) and 2F (Jan 2018) are agile SSO satellites at about 500 km with about 0.65 m panchromatic imaging and a swath near 10 km; Cartosat-2A (2008, about 1 m class) is listed operational but ageing. Several satellites tasked together raise the revisit over a target. Best for cartography, utilities, urban growth and cadastral work. Limits: cloud and darkness, narrow swath. | Resourcesat-2 / 2A: Resourcesat-2 (2011) and Resourcesat-2A (Dec 2016, the one listed operational) fly at about 817 km in SSO with three cameras: LISS-4 (5.8 m, steerable), LISS-3 (23.5 m, includes shortwave infrared) and AWiFS (56 m, about 740 km swath, about 5-day repeat).

chunks.heading: Recommendation case 81: Earth Observation (Optical) / Global / LEO / Continuous
chunks.text: | Resourcesat-2 / 2A: Resourcesat-2 (2011) and Resourcesat-2A (Dec 2016, the one listed operational) fly at about 817 km in SSO with three cameras: LISS-4 (5.8 m, steerable), LISS-3 (23.5 m, includes shortwave infrared) and AWiFS (56 m, about 740 km swath, about 5-day repeat). Best for crop acreage, forest cover, water bodies and land use. Limits: moderate resolution, cloud cover. | HySIS: Hyperspectral Imaging Satellite launched 29 Nov 2018 on PSLV-C43, SSO about 636 km. Records about 55 contiguous bands across visible-near-infrared and shortwave infrared at about 30 m, which allows identification of minerals, crop stress, vegetation type and coastal conditions. Limits: modest resolution and swath, limited tasking, large data volumes. | Oceansat-3 (EOS-06): Launched 26 Nov 2022 on PSLV-C54, SSO about 720 km. Carries OCM-3 (13-band ocean colour with a very wide swath of over 1,000 km), SSTM (thermal sea-surface temperature), SCAT-3 (Ku-band scatterometer for ocean-surface wind) and ARGOS (data collection).

chunks.heading: Recommendation case 81: Earth Observation (Optical) / Global / LEO / Continuous
chunks.text: Carries OCM-3 (13-band ocean colour with a very wide swath of over 1,000 km), SSTM (thermal sea-surface temperature), SCAT-3 (Ku-band scatterometer for ocean-surface wind) and ARGOS (data collection). chunks.heading: Recommendation case 101: Earth Observation (Optical) / Regional / LEO / Continuous
chunks.text: | HySIS: Hyperspectral Imaging Satellite launched 29 Nov 2018 on PSLV-C43, SSO about 636 km. Records about 55 contiguous bands across visible-near-infrared and shortwave infrared at about 30 m, which allows identification of minerals, crop stress, vegetation type and coastal conditions. Limits: modest resolution and swath, limited tasking, large data volumes. | Oceansat-3 (EOS-06): Launched 26 Nov 2022 on PSLV-C54, SSO about 720 km. Carries OCM-3 (13-band ocean colour with a very wide swath of over 1,000 km), SSTM (thermal sea-surface temperature), SCAT-3 (Ku-band scatterometer for ocean-surface wind) and ARGOS (data collection). Gives about 2-day coverage. Best for chlorophyll, algal blooms, fishery advisories, cyclone winds and sea-surface temperature. Limits: coarse over land. | EOS-08: Launched 16 Aug 2024 on SSLV-D3; a 175 kg microsatellite in a 475 km orbit inclined about 37 degrees. Payloads: EOIR (visible, mid-wave and long-wave infrared for day and night imaging, fire and volcano monitoring), GNSS-R (ocean wind, soil moisture, flood inundation) and an ultraviolet dosimeter supporting Gaganyaan.

chunks.heading: Recommendation case 161: Synthetic Aperture Radar / Global / LEO / Continuous
chunks.text:
- Application: Synthetic Aperture Radar
- Coverage: Global
- Requested orbit: LEO
- Requested revisit: Continuous
- Resolved orbit: LEO
- Feasibility: P (partial)
- Recommended ISRO satellites: NISAR, RISAT-1A (global); RISAT-2B family (about +/-45 deg latitude only)
- Best achievable revisit (hours): 144.0
- Revisit fit: Does not meet
- Rationale: Only NISAR/RISAT-1A provide beyond-tropics coverage.
- Alternative if unavailable:
- Combination members: NISAR + RISAT-1A (EOS-04) + RISAT-2B / 2BR1 / EOS-01
- Combination details: NISAR: NASA-ISRO radar observatory of about 2,400 kg launched 30 Jul 2025 on GSLV-F16, operational since 7 Nov 2025. Orbit about 747 km, 98.4 degrees, 6 am / 6 pm crossing. NASA supplies the L-band SAR (24 cm) and a 12 m mesh reflector; ISRO supplies the S-band SAR (10 cm), the satellite bus and the launch. SweepSAR gives a 242 km swath at 3 to 10 m with an exact 12-day repeat, in single, dual and quad polarisation; data are free and open. Best for biomass, soil moisture, ground deformation, glaciers, sea ice, floods and crops.

chunks.text: Best for biomass, soil moisture, ground deformation, glaciers, sea ice, floods and crops. Limits: systematic rather than on demand, no daily revisit. | RISAT-1A (EOS-04): Launched 14 Feb 2022 on PSLV-C52; about 1,700 kg, SSO about 529 km. C-band SAR with several modes from a few metres to about 50 m resolution and a wide swath in coarse mode; about 25-day repeat. Best for crops, soil moisture, flood mapping and forestry. Limits: coarser than X-band, slow repeat. Its sister RISAT-1B (EOS-09) was lost in the May 2025 PSLV-C61 failure. | RISAT-2B / 2BR1 / EOS-01: RISAT-2B (May 2019), RISAT-2BR1 (Dec 2019) and EOS-01 / RISAT-2BR2 (Nov 2020, status to verify) carry X-band SAR on a 3.6 m radial-rib antenna in LEO inclined about 37 degrees at roughly 550 to 580 km. Spotlight, strip and wider modes reach sub-metre to a few metres. The inclined orbit gives repeated passes over India and the tropics, so this is the fastest-revisit SAR family, but it does not reach polar latitudes. Best for defence, borders, ship detection, floods and disaster response.

chunks.text: Second-generation NVS satellites add an L1 signal for interoperability with GPS and Galileo and indigenous rubidium clocks. Capability is reduced until NVS-03 and later satellites are launched.

Gives about 2-day coverage. Best for chlorophyll, algal blooms, fishery advisories, cyclone winds and sea-surface temperature. Limits: coarse over land. | Together: Polar Oceansat-3 and the tropical, inclined EOS-08 sample winds, sea state, sea-surface temperature and soil moisture at different times and latitudes, improving coverage over India and the Indian Ocean.

- Best achievable revisit (hours): 12.0

- Rationale: Orbit tracks converge near the poles, giving several passes per day at high latitude; optical OCM is limited by polar night, scatterometer and thermal sensors continue.

Limits: coarse over land. | Together: Oceansat-3 supplies ocean colour, sea-surface temperature and wind with near-polar coverage, filling the gap that geostationary INSAT satellites leave at the poles and over detailed ocean parameters.

Radar altimetry by satellite is a technique used in oceanography to measure, globally over the oceans, the sea level needed to understand ocean circulation and its variability. The importance of altimetry data to better understand the ocean circulation and its impact on the climate of the Earth led to the TOPEX/Poseidon and Jason series of satellites complemented by ERS1-2, GFO and ENVISAT.

The importance of altimetry data to better understand the ocean circulation and its impact on the climate of the Earth led to the TOPEX/Poseidon and Jason series of satellites complemented by ERS1-2, GFO and ENVISAT. With the launch of these missions began a data collection that must continue well into the century in order to monitor the inter-annual evolution and separate transient phenomena from secular variations. SARAL/AltiKa mission belongs to the global altimetry system and then participates to the precise and accurate observations of ocean circulation and sea surface elevation for its life time. Thus it is the aim of AltiKa part of the SARAL mission to provide altimetric measurements designed to study ocean circulation and sea surface elevation with the same accuracy as the one provided by ENVISAT mission and complementary to Jasons mission. The AltiKa project developed by CNES is based on a large Ka-band altimeter (35.75 GHz, 500MHz), 1st oceanographic altimeter using such a high frequency.

The AltiKa project developed by CNES is based on a large Ka-band altimeter (35.75 GHz, 500MHz), 1st oceanographic altimeter using such a high frequency. The use of the Ka-band frequency will supply more accurate measurements (improvement of the spatial and vertical resolution) enabling a better observation of ices, coastal areas, continental water bodies as well as the waves height. The drawback of this Ka-band frequency is its sensitivity to rain that can lead to signal attenuation. The SARAL/AltiKa mission is part of the operational satellite altimetry system, jointly with Jason-2, and enables to ensure the service continuity which is nowadays provided by ENVISAT altimeter jointly with Jason-2 and Jason-1. chunks.heading: About the role
chunks.text: Scientist/Engineer, Mechanical/Aerospace: Design and test launch vehicles, propulsion hardware, spacecraft structures, thermal systems and mechanisms. Related career goal: Rocket and launch vehicle engineering. This role is in the group: Engineering.

chunks.heading: Education needed
chunks.text: Typical study route: B.E./B.Tech or other specified degree in Mechanical, Aerospace or an accepted related discipline; higher study may help for specialist roles. Education path: Class 11–12 Science with PCM, then B.E./B.Tech Mechanical or Aerospace, or another accepted discipline. Check the latest official advertisement for accepted degrees, minimum marks and age.

chunks.heading: Exams and selection
chunks.text: There is no one common ISRO entrance exam for all jobs. ISRO's Centralised Recruitment Board (ICRB) and individual centres advertise different positions and may use different selection methods. Scientist/Engineer 'SC' (engineering graduates): Depending on the recruitment advertisement, selection may be through a written/computer-based test and interview, through GATE-score-based shortlisting and interview, or another method stated in that notice. Some recruitment drives combine different routes for different vacancies. Do not assume GATE is compulsory for every Scientist/Engineer post, and do not assume GATE alone guarantees selection. Prepare the core subjects for your engineering branch, engineering mathematics where relevant, and previous papers for the exact post/discipline. The official ICRB advertisement is the authority for accepted degrees, minimum marks, age, selection stages and dates. GATE (Graduate Aptitude Test in Engineering): Useful for engineering and some science-related recruitment routes when the specific ISRO notice accepts a GATE score.

chunks.heading: Exams and selection
chunks.text: GATE (Graduate Aptitude Test in Engineering): Useful for engineering and some science-related recruitment routes when the specific ISRO notice accepts a GATE score. Choose the GATE paper that matches your discipline and the advertisement's requirements. Preparation: core undergraduate subjects, engineering mathematics where applicable, previous GATE papers, timed mock tests and error analysis. Check the current year's official GATE website for the relevant cycle. Official site: https://gate2026. iitg. ac. in/

chunks.heading: Subjects and books
chunks.text:
All engineering candidates: Mathematics and core subjects required by the specific branch; use your university's standard textbooks and official syllabus. Mechanical / Aerospace: Engineering mechanics, strength of materials, thermodynamics, fluid mechanics, heat transfer, propulsion-related basics, control and structures as applicable. Suggested standard books for Scientist/Engineer, Mechanical/Aerospace (ASTRAAI suggestions, not from the ISRO guide):
- Advanced Engineering Mathematics by Erwin Kreyszig
- Higher Engineering Mathematics by B. S. Grewal
- Introduction to Flight by John D. Anderson Jr.
- Rocket Propulsion Elements by George P. Sutton and Oscar Biblarz
- Engineering Thermodynamics by P. K. Nag
- Fluid Mechanics by Frank M. White
- Mechanics of Materials by Ferdinand Beer and E. Russell Johnston
- Orbital Mechanics for Engineering Students by Howard D. Curtis Book selection note (from the guide): use the books prescribed by your degree programme and standard references for your branch.

chunks.heading: Subjects and books
chunks.text: Book selection note (from the guide): use the books prescribed by your degree programme and standard references for your branch. The official syllabus and past papers should decide what to prioritise; avoid buying large sets of books before identifying the target exam.

chunks.heading: Study resources
chunks.text:
- Official ISRO Careers: Recruitment notifications, eligibility, career information, fellowships and old question papers. https://www. isro. gov. in/ISRO_EN/Careers. html
- ISRO Current Opportunities: Centre-wise and centralised vacancies, application dates and detailed notices. https://www. isro. gov. in/CurrentOpportunities. html
- ISRO old question papers: Previous papers published for particular disciplines and posts; availability varies. https://www. isro. gov. in/ISRO_EN/Careers. html
- NPTEL: Free learning materials and courses in engineering mathematics, thermodynamics, fluids, electronics, control systems, programming and algorithms. https://nptel. ac. in/
- GATE official portal: Use the official website for the current exam year, syllabus, papers and dates; the 2026 portal is linked here as a reference. https://gate2026. iitg. ac. in/

chunks.heading: Roadmap
chunks.text: Step 1, education: Class 11–12 Science with PCM, then B.E./B.Tech Mechanical or Aerospace, or another accepted discipline. Step 2, choose one target post and read its latest official advertisement from beginning to end. Six-month foundation plan: Month 1: Review mathematics and fundamentals of the chosen discipline; read the target recruitment syllabus. Month 2: Cover the first major core subjects and practise topic-wise questions. Month 3: Continue core subjects and work through numerical and conceptual problems. Month 4: Finish high-priority topics and begin solving previous recruitment papers. Month 5: Take timed mock tests; analyse mistakes and revise weak areas. Month 6: Practise full papers, revise formulas and confirm the latest recruitment eligibility and selection method. Suggested daily routine: 1 to 2 hours of core subjects, 30 minutes of problem-solving and 15 minutes reviewing mistakes. Adapt this to your semester schedule and exam date. Preparing for selection: Choose one target post and read its latest official advertisement from beginning to end.

chunks.heading: Roadmap
